The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

- 🎧 The DOJ wants California to segregate ballots of those on its list and to delay counting them until investigations are complete. Election law experts doubt the DOJ will succeed, given its past attempts to change state voting processes, Miles Parks tells Up First. He adds that it would be surprising to see a shift just two weeks before the election with ballots already distributed. Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Experts tell Parks they are concerned that federal law enforcement might use accusations to confiscate ballots during counting, but many local voting officials are preparing by keeping county attorneys on speed dial.

Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.

- 🎧 Trump's rally in Kansas and trip to North Carolina aren't where the leader of the Republican Party's attention should be, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and many Republican groups have ceased ad spending in North Carolina, viewing the Senate race as a lost cause. Republicans are prioritizing efforts to save their Senate majority over saving the House majority, while Democrats are capitalizing on opportunities in conservative areas, Fowler says. In Georgia, with a million voters already casting ballots, Fowler says he sees an increase in Black voter turnout in the state and across the South.

TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns about the app's risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show employees' frustration with leadership's response to these issues. Depositions filed in March 2026 provide new insights into TikTok's child safety measures since its surge in popularity in 2018. Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.

Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

- 🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.

- 🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
- 🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.
- 🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.

Trump makes Russia-friendly moves as he looks for a way to end the war with Ukraine
President Trump's up and down relationship with Russia is back on as he presses to find an end to the war in Ukraine amid high energy costs ahead of the U.S. midterms.
Democrats and Republicans are opposed to President Trump's friendlier stance toward Russia.

Senators from both parties are criticizing Trump's decision to lift diesel sanctions. The president said that move was meant to head off high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections. He's also paused sharing military intelligence with Ukraine. In a moment, we'll discuss all this with former U.S. Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul. We begin with the news.
MARTÍNEZ: NPR's Emily Feng is with us this morning. Emily, so first, run through what President Trump has done to roll back pressure on Russia.

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: OK. Here's just a brief list. He's had the Treasury Department lift sanctions on Russian diesel. He's effectively suspended a sanctions bill he just signed into law that was named in honor of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. He said yesterday he was willing to sit down with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin to talk about the war on Ukraine even if Ukraine's leader is not there. And then he cited a Ukrainian woman he heard speak about the loss of lives as a reason to end the war.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: She blamed Zelenskyy. She said, he's killing our men. And the fact is, she said - and it was very poignant. She said, our men are dying. Our men have no legs.

FENG: Also last week, Ukrainian officials say they lost connectivity for a few days to Starshield and Starlink. These are satellite services which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says he thinks the U.S. was behind that. And he also made the extraordinary move of lobbying a bipartisan group of senators and House members about this Starlink issue this week.
MARTÍNEZ: Emily, do you have any sense why Trump, who really has faced repeated accusations of favoring Russia, is now seemingly courting Russia again?

FENG: Trump wants a deal. He wants a foreign policy win in Ukraine. And he told reporters yesterday he is negotiating with Russia on a number of issues - on energy, on American hostages in Russia. And he also wants to keep Russia from - not helping Iran. So he said he doesn't want to drive Russia away from the bargaining table.
I spoke to Bill Taylor about this. He was a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine until 2009. And Taylor notes the U.S. is no longer giving much direct financial and military assistance to Ukraine.

BILL TAYLOR: I mean, it's down 95%. The only thing we continue to provide, which is very valuable - it's come up in the last couple of days - is this military intelligence and the ability for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States and Elon Musk to be able to provide Starlink.

FENG: But now the U.S. has shown Ukraine cannot rely on the U.S. for that intelligence either. And in that meeting I mentioned with members of Congress on Monday, Zelenskyy said that the administration, the U.S. government, is the one holding up weapons for his country.
PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We also know that, unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for.

FENG: Secretary of State Marco Rubio also spoke on this. Speaking in Mumbai, India, today, Rubio said it could be accurate that a batch of interceptors purchased for Ukraine has not been delivered. Rubio, however, told reporters that the important takeaway was, quote, "there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."
MARTÍNEZ: All right. So, Emily, there's been a bipartisan fallout that's followed this. Tell us about that.

FENG: Yes. Notably, both Republican and Democratic lawmakers are criticizing the U.S. for buying Russian diesel. For example, on top of the lawmakers that Zelenskyy briefed, you have Republican Representative Mike Lawler saying the diesel puts money in Russia's pocket. Notably, Darline Graham, sister of the late Senator Graham, whose namesake sanctions law was just signed into law by Trump, spoke out against the U.S. buying Russian diesel. And this fallout is illustrative of the bind that Trump has put himself in by starting a seemingly intractable conflict with Iran. He has driven up energy prices for Americans. That's put more leverage in Russia's hands to push the U.S. for a quick resolution on Ukraine.
MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Emily Feng. Emily, thanks.
Former U.S. ambassador on Trump's recent moves to embrace Russia
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former U.S. Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul about President Trump's latest embrace of Russia and what it means for Ukraine and any hopes of peace.

Let's ask Michael McFaul about this. He was the U.S. ambassador to Russia during the Obama administration and is now a professor of political science and a Hoover senior fellow at Stanford University, where it is ridiculously early, and yet he's gotten up to talk with us. Ambassador, welcome.
INSKEEP: And thanks for the time. The president has been so favorable to Russia that I have to ask if you think that his most recent actions amount to a shift at all.

MCFAUL: Well, you're right to remind everybody that he's liked Putin for a long time. I mean, go back to the beginning of his first administration. He constantly praised Putin. He sided with him. When questioned in a very famous summit with Putin, his first one in 2018, in Helsinki, he sided with Putin and he didn't side with our own intelligence community about whether there was interference in our elections.

So that piece has been consistent. What I think has changed in a profound way in the last week - in a profound, tragic way for me - is he always had a few constraints. He always was talking to Zelenskyy. He claimed from Day 1 of this second term that he wanted to end the war in Ukraine. And I applaud him for that, by the way. Everybody should want to see the end of this barbaric war that Putin started. But this week felt different in both tone and actions.

So rhetorically, he's always sided with Putin. Now he really doubled down. As Emily just went through that list, every single one of those things are concessions to Putin. That's not a way to mediate. He's not mediating. He's just giving Putin what he wants. And then when it comes to Zelenskyy, he's blaming Zelenskyy for Putin killing his own people. And I thought that clip you just played of the Ukrainian woman, it's a former press secretary of President Zelenskyy, who's now defected, gone - you know, just doesn't support Zelenskyy anymore, I should be clear...
MCFAUL: I think you just see the true colors of President Trump right now.

INSKEEP: Well, Zelenskyy spoke with this bipartisan group of American lawmakers yesterday, and he posted a video online afterward of his address. He said the Pentagon is making it harder for Ukraine to get intelligence and also delaying the U.S. approval of the transfer of weapons. Let's listen to some of that.
PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us. And this is in sharp contrast to what we are achieving on the battlefield.

INSKEEP: I want to explore that a little bit, too, because he says a political decision, suggesting it's not just Trump's impulses here or there, but that there's a deliberate change in policy by the United States. It sounds like you would agree with that.

MCFAUL: I do. And I tragically agree with that because we in this fight between democratic Ukraine and autocratic Russia, in this fight between an imperial leader in Russia who's invading and trying to reconquer a former colony, we're now on the side of the autocrats. This is unprecedented in American history. I can't think of a time when in a similar kind of situation, in 100 years, where we have decided, oh, we're going to support the autocrats, the imperialists against a country fighting for its independence with a democratically elected leader.

Now, you know, there's some ambiguity as to who made the decision about turning off Starlink. And there's some ambiguity about why there's the delays in the missiles, the interceptors that President Zelenskyy is talking about. But if we were trying to help Ukraine, we would be clearing up that ambiguity. We would be saying, this is what happened, and now we're turning it on. And Trump is doing exactly the opposite.
INSKEEP: Well, let's talk about some of those people.
MCFAUL: And I just find that the moral...
INSKEEP: Let's talk about some of those people in the room with Zelenskyy...
INSKEEP: ...Some of those lawmakers from both parties, some of whom face the voters...
INSKEEP: ...In a couple of weeks. What, if anything, can they do about the president's course?

MCFAUL: Well, in the short run, not much. But in the short run, I guarantee you, most of them are not going to be lining up with the president, because the public opinion polling here in America about Putin is very clear. We don't have many polls, Steve, where 80% of Americans - 83% of Americans think that Putin's a bad guy. So when Trump is embracing him, he is out of step with American society.
INSKEEP: You said in the short term. What about the longer term? Is there something Congress can do over time?

MCFAUL: Yes. I hope when there's a new Congress - and, you know, tragically, that's a long time for Ukrainians. But introduce new legislation to prevent Americans from doing business with Russia. Introduce new legislation to provide a new military assistance package to Ukraine. We haven't had that for two years. And even if President Trump vetoes it, it'll at least show what side the U.S. Congress is on.
INSKEEP: And I guess we should mention Congress did pass a law, but it allowed the president to waive it, and that's what he's done.
INSKEEP: I suppose Congress would have to pass a law with more restrictions.
INSKEEP: Ambassador McFaul, it's always a pleasure talking with you. Thank you so much.
INSKEEP: Michael McFaul is a former U.S. ambassador to Russia.

Joe Cordina: Former boxing world champion cleared of assaulting man he punched outside petrol station
Two-time IBF super-featherweight champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station; a district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault
Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station.
A district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault by beating against Jamie O'Brien, 33, following a trial at Cardiff Magistrates' Court.
The court heard Cordina had been filling up his Land Rover at Pentwyn service station in Cardiff in February when he noticed O'Brien staring at him.
Cordina, a two-time IBF super-featherweight champion, approached O'Brien - who was sitting on the pavement near the station exit - believing he was a fan.
Judge Charlotte Murphy described how O'Brien then "shoulder barged him to the chest and chin", in what she found was a "deliberate assault" on Cordina.
She highlighted that the attack had taken place just two weeks after Cordina had been told by police that there was a threat to his life.
In her ruling, the judge said: "I am satisfied that the defendant believed it was necessary to use force to defend himself.
"I am further satisfied that a single, measured, controlled punch was proportionate in the circumstances.
"It is very easy to consider the defendant's response by considering the CCTV in slow motion, however the defendant had a split second to consider his response to the shoulder barge."
The judge said she accepted Cordina's evidence that he had repeatedly pushed O'Brien "while on the floor to keep him away from him".
"In my view, it was necessary and the force used was proportionate in the circumstances," she added.
"I reject any suggestion that the defendant was retaliating in any way.
"This is a person who has lived in the public eye for many years and has interacted with the public on a daily basis.
"For all of those reasons, the crown has not proved to the criminal standard. I therefore find the defendant not guilty and dismiss the charge."
The judge had previously ruled there was no case to answer in relation to the second charge of assault.
CCTV footage played to the court showed O'Brien pushing Cordina with his shoulder, before Cordina punched him.
O'Brien, from Pentwyn, previously pleaded guilty to a charge of assault by beating.
Police began to investigate the incident after footage was circulated online. The judge ruled on Tuesday there was no evidence that O'Brien knew the person who was filming.
She added that Cordina had approached O'Brien "in good faith", believing he was a fan.
During the trial, Cordina said he initially thought O'Brien wanted a photograph and described how he was accustomed to being recognised four or five times a day.
He told the court he had acted in self-defence because he felt threatened after O'Brien assaulted him.
"He had his hands in his pockets, I don't know what people carry on them these days," Cordina said.
After the case, Cordina's lawyer Nadeem Majid issued a statement to the media.
He said: "Today's verdict is a huge relief for Joe and everybody who is close to him.
"He has always maintained he is innocent throughout this.
"On behalf of Joe, I'd like to thank his family, his friends, his loyal fans, his legal team for their unwavering support through what's clearly been a very difficult time.
"Joe would now like to concentrate on his family and in particular his boxing. We'd all like to see him on the bill in December. Thank you all very much."

The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse.

However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes, you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem.
Why are bright screens bad for stargazing?
When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision.

However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas.
One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option.
The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light.
How to block white light in stargazing apps

Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps:
SkyView: Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red.
Star Walk 2: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode.
Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode.

All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock.
If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone.
How to block white light on Android phones
On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have.
One near-universal option is to dim your smartphone. Swipe down the notification panel from the top of the screen and you'll see a brightness slider. Slide this to the left to dim your phone.

We'd also recommend disabling adaptive brightness in the Display section of your phone's settings. You may also have an Extra Dim option in the Accessibility menu — just don't dim the screen to the point of not being able to see it at all!

Some Android phones, such as recent Samsung and Google Pixel models, also offer a Red Filter. On some, you'll find this in Accessibility, then Vision Enhancements, then Color Filter. You can then choose the color you want and also tweak the opacity.
All the above options will let you continue to use your smartphone for stargazing, while minimizing its negative impact on your night vision.
How to block white light on Apple iPhones

As with Android phones, iPhones have a built-in option to dim the screen brightness. In this case, you swipe down from the top of the screen and look for the vertical brightness slider, represented by a sun icon. Reduce the slider as much as you're comfortable with, dimming the screen while still keeping it visible.
Beyond that, recent iPhones also offer the ability to apply a color filter, again via their Accessibility options. Here's how to do that.

First, tap on the Settings icon, then pick Accessibility. Select Display & Text Size and go to Color Filters. Tap the Color Filter button. Then, pick Color Tint and move the Hue and Intensity sliders all the way to the right.

If you were approaching the edge of a spiral galaxy, arriving from afar through the cosmos, it might look something like this.

In this new snapshot by the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS), we can see the edge of the spiral galaxy NGC 1827. Found about 37 million light-years from Earth, this galaxy sparkles in this side-on view.

Not all spiral galaxies are the same. This galaxy is what is known as an "intermediate" spiral, which means that its structure sits somewhere between that of a barred and unbarred spiral galaxy. Barred galaxies have a distinctive central, bar-shaped structure, while the unbarred variety lacks this bar and can look more like circular spirals.
NGC 1827's spiral shape isn't clear from the side, however. From this perspective, we see its twinkling edge, speckled with stars and woven together with brown ribbons of dust.

Beneath the beauty of this spiral edge lies an expansive, cosmic landscape. Bright blue stars dot the spiral's side, with one particularly luminous star taking the spotlight with four diffraction spikes — created by light bending through the inner workings of Hubble's camera — emanating from its center.

This image was captured as part of a larger Hubble survey that's exploring 260 satellite galaxies, which are galaxies gravitationally bound to larger hosts. Hubble is specifically looking to survey satellite galaxies that lie near host galaxies similar to our own Milky Way.
So far, Hubble has spotted 111 such satellites and will continue to observe, hunting for the rest.

By studying satellite galaxies like this one, which also happens to be an especially low-mass galaxy, researchers could better understand the complicated dynamics both within the galaxies themselves and between them and their host galaxies.
The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached.

For years, space sustainability experts have warned that the growing number of satellites in orbit and the quantity of dead metal left behind threatens to trigger a dangerous cascade of collisions known as the Kessler Syndrome. Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe.

The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think. Humankind's utilization of space is at an inflection point, as companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin and Amazon plan to launch constellations of hundreds of thousands of telecommunication satellites and orbiting data centers in the coming years.

"Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors," Daniel Kaffine, a professor of environmental and resource economics at University of Colorado Boulder, told Space.com.

"Waiting until it gets really, really bad to start implementing any of these types of policy interventions has historically been what we have done," Kaffine added. "But maybe we can think about things we can do right now."

In a paper published last month in the journal Nature Communications, Kaffine and his collaborators propose a scheme that would require satellite operators to post a bond of $200,000 before launch, refundable with interest upon the completion of a successful deorbit. Companies that fail to remove their junk would lose the money, which could go toward a shared pool funding active debris-removal missions, the researchers said.
"You could possibly raise billions of dollars by that," said Kaffine. "We think it's a very neat policy that doesn't require international coordination."

International bodies, such as the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee, ask satellite operators to remove their spacecraft from orbit within 25 years after the mission's end. The American Federal Communications Commission (FCC) imposes an even stricter standard — a five-year requirement for satellites in low Earth orbit. Still, a staggering 60% of satellites remain in place when their propellant runs out, the researchers say, as no consequences ensue if they fail to deorbit.

Solving the problem on the international level would be difficult, as international bodies have no powers to enforce compliance. Moreover, the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), which sets down rules for the peaceful exploration of outer space, requires the unanimous support of every member state to pass new regulations, which is nearly impossible to achieve.

"The policy we propose could be implemented on a national level, which is why we think it's interesting," Indigo Brownhall, a space sustainability researcher at University College London and the paper's lead author, told Space.com. "Any country in Europe can request satellites registered with them to follow this bond policy."

To put it simply, no satellite registered in a given country gets to space before putting the money into the kitty. The researchers acknowledge that it might be hard to persuade major players historically averse to regulations, such as the U.S., to roll out such a scheme. But they say a more environmentally conscious block, like the European Union (EU), could enforce compliance by limiting market access to those who observe their rules.

"The consumer market in Europe is massive, like 300 to 400 million people," Brownhall said. "And the EU can request anyone who wants to sell space data or any products in the EU to follow their rules. They did this with GDPR [General Data Protection Regulation]. And you can imagine that somebody like Starlink [SpaceX's satellite-internet subsidiary] surely wants to sell Starlink terminals to Europeans."
The authors estimate that, even if the scheme only covered 20% of global satellite launches, it would reduce the number of derelict satellites careening around the planet by 18%.

Currently, more than 57,000 pieces of space debris larger than 4 inches (10 centimeters) hurtle around Earth completely out of control, according to estimates by the European Space Agency. That's double the figure from less than 10 years ago. Most of these fragments were generated by explosions and orbital collisions that shattered satellites and used rocket stages into clouds of dangerous debris.

"Leaving big satellites that no longer work up there is like a ticking time bomb," Brownhall said. "Active satellites can move out of the way, but when two derelict satellites are going to hit each other, there is nothing you can do but watch it."
Kaffine said the policy could be modelled on U.S. oil operators' bond scheme, in place since the 1960s, which ensures that oil giants plug used oil wells after ceasing extraction.

"If the oil operators clean up after completing the oil production job, they get the money back," said Kaffine. "If they don't, the money goes into a fund, which the government then uses to clean up orphan wells. It's quite an analogous situation to what we see in space."

In the meantime, evidence of the worsening orbital situation is coming thick and fast. Space situational awareness companies such as U.S.-based LeoLabs, which use networks of ground-based radars and telescopes to monitor traffic in space, report increasing numbers of disintegration events — incidents involving either an explosion or a collision between old satellites, fragments and rocket bodies. In the past six months, LeoLabs has reported at least four fragmentation events in space, which together created hundreds of new pieces of space debris.

Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain

- Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

Statins are among the most important medications for preventing cardiovascular disease. By lowering cholesterol, they have helped save millions of lives and reduce the likelihood of heart attacks and strokes. However, these benefits can come with unwanted effects. Some patients develop muscle pain or weakness, while a small number experience serious muscle breakdown that can potentially cause kidney failure.

Scientists at the University of British Columbia (UBC), working with colleagues at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, have identified a molecular mechanism that helps explain these complications. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, could guide the development of safer statins that maintain their cholesterol-lowering benefits while minimizing muscle damage.
How Statins Trigger a Harmful Calcium Leak

To investigate what happens inside muscle cells, the researchers used cryo-electron microscopy, an advanced imaging method that allows scientists to examine protein structures in remarkable detail. Their investigation centered on the ryanodine receptor (RyR1), a protein that regulates the movement of calcium within muscle cells.

Under normal conditions, this protein functions as a controlled gateway, releasing calcium when muscles need to contract. The researchers found that statins can interfere with this process by holding the channel open. As a result, calcium escapes continuously into areas where it should be carefully regulated, creating conditions that can injure muscle tissue.

"We were able to see, almost atom by atom, how statins latch onto this channel," said lead author Dr. Steven Molinarolo, a postdoctoral researcher in UBC's department of biochemistry and molecular biology. "That leak of calcium explains why some patients experience muscle pain or, in extreme cases, life-threatening complications."

The researchers concentrated on atorvastatin, a commonly prescribed medication for lowering cholesterol. Although this particular drug was the main focus, their results suggest that similar interactions could occur with other medications in the statin family.

One of the most striking discoveries was the unusual way statin molecules attach to the calcium channel. Rather than acting individually, three molecules occupy a specific pocket within the protein. The first binds while the channel is closed, making it more likely to open. Two additional molecules then enter the pocket and hold the channel open, allowing calcium to continue leaking.

"This is the first time we've had a clear picture of how statins activate this channel," said Dr. Filip Van Petegem, senior author and professor at UBC's Life Sciences Institute. "It's a big step forward because it gives us a roadmap for designing statins that don't interact with muscle tissue."

This detailed understanding could give drug developers a way to address the problem at its source. By modifying the specific features of statin molecules that interfere with muscle proteins, scientists may be able to reduce unwanted effects without compromising the drugs' ability to control cholesterol.

More than 200 million people worldwide use statins. Although severe muscle injury occurs in only a small percentage of patients, less serious problems such as soreness, weakness, and fatigue are considerably more widespread. These symptoms can be disruptive enough that some people discontinue their medication, potentially losing important protection against cardiovascular disease.

The discovery could eventually help researchers create treatments that are easier to tolerate, allowing more patients to continue taking medications that reduce their risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Achieving this level of understanding required exceptionally detailed imaging. Working with the high-resolution macromolecular cryo-electron microscopy facility at UBC's faculty of medicine, the team was able to observe precisely how statin molecules interact with the muscle protein. These structural insights connect a longstanding drug safety concern to a specific molecular process, providing valuable information for future medication development.
"Statins have been a cornerstone of cardiovascular care for decades," Dr. Van Petegem said. "Our goal is to make them even safer, so patients can benefit without fear of serious side effects."

Although additional research and drug development will be needed before these findings translate into new treatments, they offer a promising direction. For millions of people who depend on statins to protect their hearts, future medications with fewer muscle-related complications could make treatment more comfortable and improve everyday quality of life.

Hurricane warning maps are improving, but a dangerous problem remains

- A new study reveals that improved hurricane forecast graphics may help people identify threatened areas without making them more likely to recognize the danger or take protective action. Researchers also found that a widespread misunderstanding of the hurricane cone persists, highlighting a potentially dangerous gap between accurate forecasts and public preparedness.

An updated hurricane forecast map is making it easier for people to identify areas threatened by storms, but new research reveals a concerning limitation. Even when people can recognize where hurricane watches are in effect, they may not feel more at risk or become more inclined to take precautions.

Researchers at Florida State University examined whether changes to the National Hurricane Center (NHC) forecast graphics improve public understanding of hurricane threats. The study involved faculty from the School of Communication within the College of Communication and Information and the Department of Geography.

The researchers evaluated an experimental graphic that expands the traditional hurricane forecast cone to include tropical storm and hurricane watches and warnings for inland areas. The familiar cone has historically placed greater emphasis on coastal regions, even though dangerous storm conditions can extend far from the shoreline.

The findings revealed mixed results. Although the revised graphic helped people without specialized weather knowledge recognize inland areas under hurricane or tropical storm watches, it did not significantly influence how dangerous they believed the storms would be or whether they intended to take protective measures. Participants also showed no improvement in identifying areas covered by storm warnings.
The updated format was developed by the NHC in 2024, and the findings were published in the American Meteorological Society journal Weather, Climate, and Society.

"The National Hurricane Center has made a number of thoughtful changes to improve how hurricane information is communicated," said Assistant Professor Elizabeth Ray, the study's lead author. "We had a simple question. Do those changes actually help people understand what the graphic is telling them about the risk they face?"
Why People Misunderstand Hurricane Forecast Maps

To investigate how the public interprets hurricane forecasts, the research team surveyed residents of Florida and Georgia. Participants were shown either the conventional hurricane cone graphic or the newer experimental version that includes additional information about inland storm threats.

People who saw the revised map were more successful at identifying locations under hurricane or tropical storm watches. However, that improvement in recognizing watch areas did not lead to greater concern about the potential danger or stronger intentions to take safety precautions.

The results also highlighted a persistent misunderstanding surrounding the familiar hurricane "cone of uncertainty." Many people incorrectly interpret the width of the cone as an indication of a storm's physical size, rather than understanding what the graphic is intended to communicate about the uncertainty in its projected track.
"For years, research has shown that people often mistake a wider cone for a bigger storm," Ray said. "Our findings suggest that even with an updated graphic, that misconception can be hard to shake."
Why Better Hurricane Warnings May Not Be Enough

The NHC introduced its expanded forecast graphic in 2024 to help people recognize that hurricane dangers are not limited to communities along the coast. Flooding, tornadoes, and destructive winds can threaten areas well inland, making it important for residents beyond coastal evacuation zones to understand their potential exposure.
By adding inland hurricane and tropical storm watches and warnings to the traditional forecast cone, the updated graphic provides a more complete picture of where dangerous conditions could develop.
However, the study suggests that adding useful information to a forecast does not automatically make people more aware of their personal risk or more likely to respond appropriately.

The researchers stressed that their findings do not call into question the quality of the NHC's weather predictions, which they consider highly accurate. Instead, the results underscore the difficulty of presenting complex meteorological information in a way that people can readily interpret and use when making safety decisions.

"Our question wasn't whether the science is good," said co-author Patrick Merle, professor and director of the School of Communication. "The science is excellent. The question is how we communicate that science so people who aren't meteorologists understand the risk they're facing.

If people find information credible but still don't understand it well enough to take protective action, then communication has fallen short. The goal is to empower people with information they can use to stay safe."
How to Better Understand Hurricane Risks

The findings point to the importance of looking beyond a single forecast image when preparing for a hurricane. Although the cone can provide valuable information about a storm's expected path, it cannot communicate every hazard that a particular community might experience.

The researchers recommend using hurricane forecast graphics alongside local weather predictions and detailed information about possible impacts. Understanding the specific threats to an area, as well as the protective steps residents should consider, can provide a more useful basis for making decisions.

"Our findings are a reminder that one graphic can only tell you part of the story," Ray said. "Don't rely on the cone alone. Pair it with clear, local information about what impacts to expect and what actions to take. That gives you a fuller picture of what the storm could mean where you live and what to do next."

Astronomers uncover new secrets of the Universeâs first five minutes
Scientists have uncovered an extraordinarily precise chemical fingerprint of the Universeâs first five minutes, revealing new clues about the Big Bang and the laws of physics.

- Scientists have achieved a major breakthrough in understanding the Universeâs earliest moments, measuring the amount of helium formed in the first five minutes after the Big Bang with unprecedented precision. Using one of the worldâs most powerful telescopes, an international team studied 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago.

Scientists have measured the amount of helium produced during the Universe's first five minutes with unprecedented precision, offering a clearer picture of the conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang. The achievement, made by an international research team that includes scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, represents a major advance in precision cosmology.

The findings, presented in five papers published in The Astrophysical Journal, are based on 130 hours of observations using the Large Binocular Telescope. By analyzing distant galaxies, the researchers reduced the uncertainty in this fundamental measurement to just 0.5%, making it three times more precise than previous estimates.

The improved accuracy provides scientists with a powerful new tool for investigating the origins of the Universe and testing the Standard Model of physics. Such fundamental tests have a long history of advancing scientific understanding and contributing to technological breakthroughs.

"This is a physics experiment on a grand scale and one of the biggest findings in my entire 40-year career," said Evan Skillman, University of Minnesota College of Science and Engineering Distinguished Professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy. "It's a fundamental number that tells us specifically about the conditions of our Universe in its first five minutes. It has diagnostic power that speaks directly to the Standard Model of Physics."

According to the Big Bang theory, the Universe began expanding from an extraordinarily hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. Three major lines of evidence support this explanation: the continuing expansion of the Universe, the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the amounts of light elements such as helium and deuterium that formed during its earliest moments.

Although cosmic expansion and the microwave background have been studied extensively, measurements of primordial helium have historically received less attention. Determining its original abundance more accurately allows researchers to investigate the physical conditions that prevailed when the Universe was only minutes old.

To achieve their new level of precision, the team departed from the conventional method of estimating primordial helium. That approach involves observing large numbers of galaxies and extrapolating the results to determine how much helium existed before later generations of stars altered their chemical composition.

Instead, the researchers selected 15 exceptionally pristine, small, distant galaxies. These galaxies have undergone relatively little chemical evolution, making them valuable cosmic "time capsules" that preserve clues about the Universe's early composition.
Powerful Telescopes Deliver Record Precision

The team used sophisticated spectrographs developed at Ohio State University to examine more than 10 helium spectral lines and 15 hydrogen lines simultaneously. Studying these signals together made it possible to identify and correct subtle sources of measurement error that earlier studies could largely overlook.
Such small effects become especially important when researchers are trying to reduce uncertainty to less than 1%. Accounting for them was essential to achieving the new 0.5% precision.

"The MODS spectrographs took 12 years to build from conception to first light on sky," said Richard Pogge, College of Arts and Sciences Distinguished Professor of Astronomy at Ohio State University. "This is the kind of project we designed them to do, and to see them deliver is enormously satisfying. It's not every day you can help build instruments that measure something fundamental about our Universe."

Beyond refining estimates of the Universe's earliest chemical composition, the new measurement provides an important test of the Standard Model of physics. The amount of helium created shortly after the Big Bang depends on the physical conditions at that time, including the types of elementary particles present.

Using their precise helium measurement, the researchers were able to calculate the number of neutrino families in the early Universe. Neutrinos are extremely light subatomic particles, and their behavior plays an important role in scientists' understanding of fundamental physics.

The results therefore do more than strengthen existing evidence for the Big Bang. They also offer a more precise way to check whether established physical theories accurately describe the Universe during its first few minutes.
"We promised a half-percent uncertainty in our proposal, and we got there," added Skillman. "In the unpredictable world of science, that doesn't happen very often."

The international collaboration brought together scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Ohio State University, Gonzaga University, Northwestern University, The University of Texas at Austin, Indiana University, University of California Santa Cruz, University of Illinois, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, and TRIUMF.

The blood vessels feeding your brain can sustain damage without an obvious warning.

Scientists have now linked higher consumption of ultraprocessed foods to signs of that damage in middle-aged adults, raising questions about how everyday eating habits relate to the brain's vascular health.
These changes can show up on brain scans even when someone has no noticeable symptoms.
Understanding their connection to diet could help researchers investigate how food choices relate to processes associated with later stroke and dementia.

The study, published in JAMA Network Open, examined dietary questionnaires, MRI scans, body fat measurements, and cognitive assessments from 8,783 adults in Canada. Participants were aged 35 to 69 and had no established cardiovascular disease.
Researchers classified reported foods by their degree of processing, investigating a category that includes many industrially formulated foods.
Among participants in the highest consumption group, approximately one in nine had MRI evidence of vascular brain injury. In the lowest consumption group, the proportion was approximately one in 12.

"These findings are important because they are established markers of cerebrovascular disease and have been associated in previous research with a higher risk of future stroke, cognitive decline, and dementia," McMaster University nutrition researcher Russell de Souza told ScienceAlert.
The scans captured two kinds of abnormalities. One involved bright areas in the brain's white matter, the tissue carrying signals between brain regions.
The other involved areas of tissue injured by interrupted blood supply, sometimes without recognizable stroke symptoms.
The association persisted in the main analysis after accounting for differences including age, smoking, exercise, income, education, hypertension, and diabetes.
Additional adjustments for body fat and fat surrounding internal organs made little difference, suggesting that adiposity alone did not explain the relationship.
Despite the differences on brain scans, ultraprocessed food intake showed no consistent association with memory and thinking test performance.
One possible explanation is that MRI can detect tissue changes before they affect abilities measured by these tests. Following participants over time could help establish whether that happened here.
"Many of the biological processes that contribute to stroke, cognitive decline, and dementia likely begin years or even decades before they become clinically apparent," de Souza said.
Heart and brain health are closely linked through the circulation supplying both organs. Habits that protect cardiovascular health may therefore also benefit the brain.
De Souza highlighted physical activity, managing blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes, and avoiding smoking as established approaches that may help reduce risk.
The dietary findings came with substantial uncertainty.

The main analysis compared ultraprocessed food servings per 2,000 calories consumed. When intake was instead calculated as a percentage of total calories or total food servings, the associations weakened and generally lost statistical significance.
Diet, brain scans, and cognitive performance were also assessed at the same visit. The study therefore cannot show whether eating patterns preceded the brain abnormalities.
Questionnaires may misclassify foods, and unmeasured differences in people's circumstances and habits could contribute to the results.
"However, the study does not establish that UPF caused the brain changes we observed," de Souza cautioned.
It also cannot separate the possible effects of industrial processing from foods' nutritional composition or the foods they replace.

To determine whether reducing ultraprocessed food consumption can change these outcomes, researchers will need studies that track participants over time and trials that deliberately change their diets.

In the brains of people with Alzheimer's and certain other types of dementia, two proteins called amyloid-beta and tau start misbehaving in different ways – though it's not clear if these abnormalities are drivers of the disease, or consequences of it.

With tau, the protein begins to misfold into the wrong shape, and collects together in threads called fibrils inside brain cells, eventually killing those cells off. A long-standing question has been how this misfolding spreads through the brain.
Now, thanks to a study published in PNAS from researchers at Northwestern University and the University of California, Santa Barbara, we may have an answer.

The study team determined that tau proteins with certain mutations are more vulnerable to misfolding, and that there's a certain 'hotspot' on these proteins that can connect them together. The hotspot repels water but is still capped by it, and when that water is released, the proteins join together in the rigid fibril shape.

"You have a certain site, and water cannot quite coat it because it doesn't like water," says physical chemist Songi Han, from Northwestern University. "But that part still needs to be protected, because if you don't, then the protein crashes out and is no longer available."
"What water tends to do is build a stabilizing cap around it and basically these water caps attract each other."

The researchers studied a fragment model of mutated tau made up of 19 amino acids, combining lab tests with computer modeling to figure out how the proteins could go from soft and shapeless initially to rigid and stacked as fibrils.
Via a docking method that happens in stages – with the first stage at the water-capped hotspot – there's a release of energy that is then used to recruit a new tau and trigger the misfolding process.

"The proteins have to misfold and neatly stack to fibrils to elongate while propagating the same misfolded shape, and the only way that this process is forever is if the same site of the protein stacks to the same," says Han.
"If you have a tiny mismatch in the alignment of the tau shapes that stack to the fibril end, the structure will eventually stop growing."

Further tests showed that when the hotspot was covered by a chemical tag, the fibrils stopped growing. While it's still very early days for the research, there's potential here for drugs that can take aim at this docking point and stop connections being made.
Left unchecked, when cells holding tau fibrils die off, those fibrils are released to then start the process in other neurons, so the problem spreads through the brain.

"Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there's always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize," says Han.
"If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating."

One of the ideas suggested by the researchers is creating synthetic tau fibrils that could be used to study the progression of Alzheimer's and dementia more generally. A better understanding of how fibrils form will be crucial to making artificial versions.

Studying abnormal tau and amyloid-beta proteins at the moment is a real challenge for researchers — getting inside the brain of a living patient is incredibly difficult to do, and in post-mortem brains donated to science all the dementia processes have stopped.

"In order to cure a disease, one needs to be able to recreate it," says Han. "There's a real problem that disease-mimicking tau fibrils cannot be synthetically made easily. It's really difficult to try to do any development with human patient tissue."
"We are trying to give the principle of how it works so that others can find solutions better, faster or more rationally."
The research has been published in PNAS.
As social media says, microplastics are this generation's lead and asbestos: useful things that seemed hunky-dory – until they weren't.
Plastics are ubiquitous because they're durable, versatile, and apparently stable.

As a result, they occupy our literal hearts and every environment, from the deep sea to ancient rocks. They've even created their own invasive-species-addled ecosystem of plastic-consuming plants and animals.
Health concerns are piling up as fast as the plastics, and new evidence suggests that these materials are not inert after all.

It's a worrying revelation for people who would rather not harbor synthetic shards in their reproductive organs: researchers from Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley, have demonstrated that microplastics become chemically active in water, catalyzing the creation of DNA-damaging free radicals.
This revelation, just published in the journal Nature, looms large given that our world is covered in water.
And guess what our bodies are mostly made of.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate [these] high-energy reactive radicals," explains first author Naixin Qian, a biotechnology chemist at Columbia University.
The researchers used multiple lab experiments, analytical techniques, and calculations to explore the reactivity of microplastics in water.
Their small size changes their properties:

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously," explains Wei Min, study co-author and head of the biomolecular-dynamics-focused Min group at Columbia University.

"Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure."

The researchers included six lab-grade, powdered common commercial plastics and delved down three lines of chemical evidence to demonstrate the formation of free radicals, specifically those of the hydroxyl type.

Made of oxygen and hydrogen, hydroxyl (OH) free radicals are among the most reactive, toxic types, whose cell-destroying prowess has helped found the booming antioxidant industry – which may not be that effective.
Based on the observations, the free radicals appear to originate from the interface of microplastics and water.

Then, when the researchers introduced lysozyme, a protein found in human bodily fluids like tears, saliva, mucus, and milk, they saw it clumping in a possibly not-so-healthy way; incidentally, protein clumps in the brain drive neurodegenerative diseases.
Adding caffeine acted as a molecular shield, halting this effect because caffeine is an antioxidant. But its protective effects are different in the lab and in the body.
The researchers also tested mouse-derived red blood cells, which were warped and fragmented by the free-radical-producing process.
Overall, the reactivity of microplastics is due to a counterintuitive cause.
The most hydrophobic (water-repelling) microplastics are the most reactive, and it's exactly due to this fact. As they repel the water, they affect its molecular structure.
This reorganization of water molecules leads to changes in electrostatic forces, which also affect cats and packing peanuts.
In short, dissolved oxygen or hydrogen ions near the hydrophobic plastic surface pick up electrons from the water's hydroxide ions, turning them into hydroxyl free radicals.
The researchers also mention the sheer number of processes that turn bulk plastics into microplastics.
In addition to industrial processes like (huge surprise) plastics manufacturing, our daily habits flood our fleshy bodies and abodes with microplastics.
Even opening and closing a water bottle abrades its cap.

"Various uses and processes in our daily lives can also generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage and IV injections in healthcare settings," says study co-author Beizhan Yan, an environmental geochemist at Columbia Climate School.
"This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."
Yan and other researchers, including co-authors from this work, are now using animal studies to ascertain how plastic particles migrate into fetal tissue during gestation.
The researchers are also exploring some ounce-of-prevention-is-worth-a-pound-of-cure avenues by testing how to reduce our exposures to tiny plastics.

Overall, the situation has sparked federal action: earlier this year the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) introduced the $144 million STOMP program to stomp out human-imbued microplastics.
One potential future solution? Changing our plastics, or at least their surfaces, because this work suggests that electrical, physical, and chemical activity happens here.

As Teresa Head-Gordon, a theoretical chemist and head of her eponymous Berkeley lab concludes, this "could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment."
The research has been published in Nature.

Quantum computers capable of doing a million reliable operations could bring about a new stage of quantum calculation. That “megaquop” regime — as it’s called — isn’t here yet. But scientists just took a significant step toward it.

A quantum computer built by the company Quantinuum has error rates so low that it could perform a million operations with only about five errors, researchers report in a paper posted October 19 on the company’s website and arXiv.org.

“These statistics are consistent with this being a good building block for that megaquop machine,” says quantum physicist David Hayes of Quantinuum, who is based in Broomfield, Colo. In order to reach that regime, however, such computers will need to be scaled up.

Quantinuum’s computer, known as Helios, is made of electrically charged atoms, called ions, hovering over a chip. Those ions serve as the 98 quantum bits, or qubits, of the computer. But, like all qubits, those ions are finicky. Their states are delicate and can flip unintentionally and mess up calculations, like a 0 randomly switching to a 1.

A technique called quantum error correction tackles this by combining multiple error-prone qubits into one, forming a supercharged unit called a logical qubit that is less prone to mistakes. (For those who grew up on 1990s TV, it’s a bit like how Captain Planet is born from the combined powers of the gang of Planeteers.)

Logical qubits come in different sizes, integrating a given number of physical qubits — the ions, in this case. Each time a logical qubit is scaled up, going, say, from seven physical qubits to 19, the error rate drops by a factor called lambda. A previous demonstration of error correction by Google, reported in Nature in 2024, had a lambda of about 2, meaning errors were cut in half each time the logical qubits were scaled up.

Quantinuum’s computer has a lambda of about 10. So errors dropped quickly when the researchers made larger logical qubits. A logical qubit composed of 37 physical qubits had just 5 errors in a million operations — close to what would be needed for the megaquop regime. However, that experiment involved only a single logical qubit. Reaching the megaquop regime could possibly involve around 50 to 100 logical qubits.

The large value of lambda means that achieving a desired error rate takes fewer physical qubits, says Ken Brown, a quantum engineer at Duke University and a scientific adviser for the company Logiqal who was not involved with the research. “That’s a huge savings in the overall number of qubits you would need. So that’s what’s exciting.”
