A major federal grant program that helps researchers purchase scientific equipment has seemingly gone dark, leaving scientists unsure of whether they will be able to apply for funding.

The National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) program provides funding for the development or acquisition of state-of-the-art, often expensive equipment that researchers use to perform fundamental science and engineering experiments. These could be for kits such as clusters of GPUs to power research into artificial intelligence, which can run into the millions of dollars to buy and install, or highly specialized lasers or microscopes. Grant applicants can ask for up to $4 million, and they must demonstrate that the equipment will be used by several groups or experiments—a condition that can make the submission process more complicated than for other grants.
In a statement released last year, the NSF said it planned to accept submissions in 2026 between October 15 and November 16. But the proposed opening date, October 15, has come and gone.

It’s the second year in a row that MRI applications have hit a speed bump. In 2025 the NSF suspended applications for the 2026 fiscal year. The agency said it had an enormous backlog of meritorious proposals from the previous year that it would consider funding instead.

When asked for comment, an NSF spokesperson said the agency is “currently working to update this funding opportunity,” but did not confirm to Scientific American when the submission process might open.

The delay comes amid numerous shakeups to federal funding of science. The Trump administration has cancelled numerous grants that had already been granted through the NSF, the National Institutes of Health and other agencies, and has attempted to introduce a major overhaul that would have granted sweeping oversight of grants to political appointees rather than the panels of experts currently in place. That change was temporarily halted in a recent government bill but could be reintroduced in December. The Trump administration has said these changes have been conducted in the name of promoting “gold standard science.”

Several people involved in submitting MRI grant applications say they have received no word from the NSF as to when the submission period for this year might open. Laura Rodman, a grant proposal consultant, says she was told by a contact at major grant consultant firm McAllister & Quinn that proposal solicitations would start shortly after the federal government’s new fiscal year began on October 1.

The lack of clarity on when, or if, the submission period will open is leaving U.S. universities and research institutions in the lurch. One grant specialist at an American university who asked to remain anonymous to protect their privacy says schools are often limited in the number of MRI grants they can apply for. In turn, universities often run their own internal, highly competitive submission process before applying—a time-consuming effort for researchers and their labs.
“Nobody knows when the deadline will be or if it will even happen, so the act of planning to apply is a gamble,” the specialist says. “Are these faculty wasting their time?”

Even the simplest grant proposal may require up at least 30 to 40 hours of preparation, according to one scientist, who also asked to remain anonymous because they currently have a proposal pending at the NSF. That workload is increased for MRI grants, because of the need to show high levels of collaboration between research teams.

“Grants are very competitive, so an investigator must write the strongest argument they can for why taxpayer funds should go to their project,” the scientist says. “Scientific instrumentation is expensive, and the NSF wants to see that a new instrument will be used regularly. Many MRI requests involve four to six scientists, which increases the coordination needed to write a compelling proposal.”
The fact that the grants are written for groups of scientists means that a delay in the submission process can ripple out and affect multiple research projects.

“If you have a broken $700,000 instrument, or an instrument that is rapidly approaching the end of its useful life, a delay could have significant consequences,” the scientist says. “Researchers may put their projects on hold, or worse, waste money on Band-Aid repairs when a replacement would be far more efficient.”
“Moreover, sometimes a few months can be the difference between a high-impact publication and getting scooped,” they add.

The delays are particularly acute given the rising concerns about the U.S. falling behind international competitors in STEM fields; the NSF is a major funding source for critical research fields, such as chemistry and physics, the scientist says.
“For researchers without National Institutes of Health funding, the MRI program is often the only available option,” they add.
One of science’s greatest strengths is its capacity to learn from mistakes. Confronted with an error, a good scientist will admit to being wrong and use the new information to learn even more.

In my January 16 The Universe column, I wrote that there are no green stars. This is because a star’s temperature governs the mix of colors of light it emits, and the way our eyes perceive that mix tips the colors to either side of the green part of the spectrum so that stars appear mostly white, blue, orange and red. The sun actually gives off most of its light in blue and green, but a variety of factors influence our perception of its color, making it appear white or perhaps slightly yellowish.
But can a star be just plain ol’ green? Nope. And I’ve been saying so for years.
WD J133001.13+643523.7 would like to have a word, however. And that word is “chartreuse.”

The white dwarf star—let’s just call it J1330 for short—really has a greenish tint, according to some interesting research published in the journal Royal Astronomical Society Techniques and Instruments on October 15. Astronomers used real observations, together with calculated models of white dwarf spectra, and, using sophisticated techniques, converted them to approximations of what our eyes would see. Surprisingly, these odd stars come in a range of delightful hues, including, yes, even green in the case of J1330.

The important change over my earlier claim is that different kinds of stars emit light in different ways. Normal stars like the sun—those still fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores—are gigantic balls of very hot ionized gas. Material in this state generally emits light across the entire visible spectrum, spread out smoothly across the rainbow of colors, from blue to red. When each color’s brightness is graphed against its wavelength, the plot (called a blackbody curve for historical reasons) resembles a lopsided bell curve that peaks at a given color, depending on the star’s temperature. Hot stars peak in the blue, cooler stars do so in the red. Some emit more green or yellow, or what have you.

Normal stars also have a thin atmosphere of ethereal gas surrounding them. Material in this gas can absorb colors at very specific wavelengths, creating dips in the blackbody spectrum. This can affect the overall color of the star—by making it slightly bluer, say, if the dilute gas preferentially absorbs red light—but the effect is minimal in essentially all cases. That is, a star’s color is completely dominated by its temperature rather than these second-order atmospheric effects.

White dwarfs, however, are different. These are compact objects that used to be the cores of stars like the sun; when a sunlike star dies, it blows off its outer layers, revealing its inner heart, which slowly cools in space over the eons like an ember from an extinguished fire. This ultradense sphere (a cubic centimeter weighs a metric ton!) is fiercely hot and holds about half the mass of the sun crammed into a volume only about that of Earth. This means white dwarfs have tremendous surface gravities, with a typical value being about 100,000 times Earth’s! Standing on the surface of a typical white dwarf, I’d weigh about 6,800 metric tons—equivalent to over 200 fully loaded semitrucks. (Did I say, “Standing”? I meant, “Squashed into a millimeter-thin smear of vapor.”)

That intense gravity means white dwarfs can have much thicker atmospheres than a normal star—thicker but squatter: most of a white dwarf’s atmosphere only reaches centimeters in altitude above the surface. But it can be very dense, on the order of a gram per cubic centimeter (about the density of liquid water). The white dwarf’s gravity is so strong, in fact, that atoms and molecules in its atmosphere can be squeezed so hard that a condition arises called “pressure broadening,” in which gas absorbs a wider range of colors than it otherwise would. All this means a white dwarf’s atmosphere can be much more efficient than a normal star’s at absorbing light emitted from below.

Combining all this information, the astronomers who did the new research examined the colors of quite a few real white dwarfs to see how they’d look to human eyes. The results were a shock to me! Some “white” dwarfs, it seems, are instead yellow, pink or purple.

Or, yes, as demonstrated by our friend J1330, they can even be green. It’s more of a chartreuse, but that counts. So there does appear to be an actual green star. And where there’s one, more are bound to exist, even if we haven’t seen them yet.

I’d love to have a good true-color image of J1330, to be honest. Unfortunately it’s a very faint star, and a decent-sized telescope would be required for the task. Even then, getting the color balance of an image right is tricky. Still, it would be fun to see it.

And I’m kicking myself; at some point I actually considered the idea that selected absorption in a stellar atmosphere might tip a star’s emissions enough to make it green but dismissed this because I was only thinking of normal stars! I’m glad these astronomers were more clever than I was.

There’s another, darker aspect to this as well. Although dense, the surface of a white dwarf is technically a fluid. The ridiculously strong gravity means that heavy elements tend to sink rapidly into the white dwarf’s interior, leaving lighter elements (such as hydrogen and helium) on the surface. Other elements, such as sodium, should readily disappear, yet that’s the exact element that makes J1330 look green! How can it exist in the atmosphere at all?
White dwarfs, it so happens, are astrophysical zombies that will happily destroy and consume their own planets.

Long after a sunlike’s star demise, some of its planets might drop down too close to the remaining white dwarf, where its ferocious tidal forces can tear them apart, shredding them into rubble. Earth has a relatively high abundance of sodium in its crust, for example, so it’s not a stretch to think rocky exoplanets should, too. Asteroids and even comets have sodium in them as well, so there’s quite a supply. If there’s a semiconstant stream of material falling onto the white dwarf, that could explain the supply of sodium that turns the tint up.

While this “polluting” of the atmosphere is a relatively common phenomenon, it takes just the right mix of planetary chunks and white dwarf temperature to produce a star that looks like J1330. So while I will happily admit to being wrong in my earlier declaration, at least one thing I said remains correct:
For stars, it’s (still) not easy being green.

Fifty years ago Richard Dawkins, a young and relatively unknown ethologist at the University of Oxford, published what would become an instant bestseller and the catalyst for his ascension as a prominent public intellectual. As its title suggests, The Selfish Gene argued that evolution is driven by selfish competition among the “fundamental particles” of inheritance: genes. The book arguably did more than any other since Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of the Species in 1859 to make evolutionary biology a hot topic of cultural conversation.

Its message seemed stark, and it still sparks controversy. We are, Dawkins argued, merely the “survival machines” of our genes, compelled by them to act in ways that promote their own interests. As those interests are selfish, so we, too, are “born selfish.” What looks like altruistic behavior, then, is merely in the service of our genes’ selfishness.

“It’s such an extraordinary book,” says evolutionary biologist Arvid Ågren, author of The Gene’s-Eye View of Evolution. “It has come to play a unique role in evolutionary biology—simultaneously influential and contentious.”

The “gene’s-eye view” of evolution introduced by Dawkins remains a central feature of modern evolutionary theory. But what that perspective reveals about the relationship of genes and organisms is still debated. One problem is that there’s no consensus about what a gene even is. “‘Gene’ is one of those words in biology that means different things in different corners of the field,” Ågren says. And whether genes are truly selfish depends on what you consider them to be.

Dawkins defined a gene in his book as “any portion of chromosomal material which potentially lasts for enough generations to serve as a unit of natural selection.” That’s not an easy sentence to parse, but it makes the gene an abstract entity defined by its evolutionary role. The definition wasn’t really Dawkins’s, as he acknowledged; other evolutionary biologists, in particular Bill Hamilton, George Williams, John Maynard Smith and Robert Trivers, had introduced the concept years prior.

But when we hear today that a gene is linked to, say, the risk of a disease, the word has a rather different meaning. Here it generally refers to a small stretch of the DNA that constitutes our genomes, typically one that encodes the chemical makeup of a protein molecule. To a developmental biologist, such a gene is a resource that cells use to make and maintain the organism. But to an evolutionary biologist, a gene is like a little agent that develops strategies over the course of evolution to ensure its own persistence.

These are very different entities, although they are connected. The evolutionary biologist doesn’t much care what a gene does, so long as it somehow affects the traits and thus the fitness of the organism. The developmental or molecular biologist doesn’t much care how a gene got to be the way it is but wants to know how it influences growth, cell function and health. And so these disparate camps may find themselves talking past each other. The question that hangs over The Selfish Gene is whether, by failing properly to acknowledge the distinction—some might even say by obscuring it—the book sowed confusion about genes.

“At the heart of this confusion lies a disciplinary conceptual divide,” says developmental biologist Alfonso Martinez Arias of Pompeu Fabra University in Spain. Evolutionary, molecular and developmental biologists all have different concepts of the gene, he says. “Dawkins only thinks about the evolutionary biology view and has little knowledge, and certainly no understanding, of molecular or developmental biology.” Reviewing The Selfish Gene in 1977, molecular biologist Gunther Stent said that Dawkins’s definition “denatures the meaningful and well-established central concept of genetics into a fuzzy and heuristically useless notion.” Dawkins, Stent said, had committed a “terminological misdemeanor” quite deliberately “to provide himself with a catchy title.”

To make matters even murkier: whether you believe genes act selfishly depends not only on which kind of “gene” you’re talking about but also on what you take “selfish” to mean. In The Selfish Gene, “there are at least four [different] uses of ‘selfish’ that we glide between,” Ågren says.

For example, Dawkins says that two “genes” could compete for the same slot on a chromosome. But these are generally regarded as variants of the same gene, called alleles. If we’re speaking about alleles, selfishness seems an apt metaphor. As Dawkins says, an allele that results in an organism with longer legs to escape predators will be more likely to survive from one generation to the next, and so it will tend to become more abundant in a population’s gene pool. That is, this “long-legged” allele multiplies at the expense of others that are less fit. Kind of selfish, right?

Then again, every distinct gene in a given genome must generally cooperate with the others if the host organism is to exist at all. Naturally, Dawkins recognizes this too. In his 2024 book The Genetic Book of the Dead, he even showed a mock-up cover of The Selfish Gene with the title changed to The Cooperative Gene, which, he said, would have been equally consistent with the book’s content. But if a word works as well as its antonym, what explanatory work is that metaphor actually doing?

The problem is that the gene that is “selfish” is not the same gene that is “cooperative.” A gene encoding one kind of protein, for instance, doesn’t really act selfishly toward a gene encoding a different protein, because their interactions are not a zero-sum game. Indeed, they probably need one another.

The real point of Dawkins’s first book is not that (evolutionary) genes are necessarily selfish, even metaphorically, but that they can be considered from an evolutionary perspective to enact strategies that enable their persistence. That makes these strategizing genes sound like wily little agents. But in considering how genes act to build and maintain an organism, they are generally nothing of the sort, not least because DNA itself is inert. It’s only over many generations that this illusion of strategic agency becomes evident. As long as we remember that this pseudoagency is purely metaphorical, there’s no problem—but invoking it (as Dawkins has) to strip actual organisms of their genuine agency is problematic, to say the least. His portrayal of organisms as passive vehicles driven by agentic genes is a fair description of the gene’s-eye model of evolution. The trouble is, this image doesn’t do justice to what organisms really are and do.

A focus on what any given model leaves out can cut both ways, however: occasional “selfish” gene conflicts really can occur. For example, genes on the sex chromosomes (X and Y in humans) can act in their own favor to skew sex ratios in a population. What’s more, there are some segments of our DNA that really do seem to act with a selfish desire to proliferate at all costs. These are typically transposons—remnants of virus DNA that can accumulate in host genomes over time. Across many generations the build-up of transposon DNA that plays no beneficial role in the health of the host organism can clog the genome and compromise the fitness of other genes. This really is “selfish DNA,” although such sequences are not in general really genes in the developmental or molecular sense as they don’t affect the traits of the organism. Instead they are often given the more neutral label “selfish genetic elements.”

Such truly selfish DNA has long been of interest to evolutionary biologists, and work on it by Trivers was a major influence on Dawkins when writing The Selfish Gene. Some biologists interpreted his book as proposing that all genes have this sort of selfishness. If that were so, the “selfish gene” hypothesis would seem now disproven in general. Most of our DNA that serves some useful biological function is best regarded as cooperative.

Among experts, then, the perception of the book’s core meaning still varies based on discipline. Some will say it’s about competition of alleles; some will say it’s about selfish genetic elements; some will say it’s just a metaphor (but for what?); and some will say it simply means genes don’t care about one another (which is just another metaphor and is, in any event, not what “selfish” means).

That Dawkins’s book is written so beautifully perhaps disinclines most readers from worrying about such distinctions. But is that a problem? Given that understanding what genes are and what they do is more important than ever in our modern age of gene editing, genomic selection of embryos and an alarming resurgent interest in eugenics, the legacy of The Selfish Gene on its half centenary is complicated. Some researchers feel that its evolutionary message remains illuminating, while others, like Martinez Arias, worry that it has sown confusion about what our genes are really up to.

All this is to say that despite (or even because of) its myriad interpretive confusions, The Selfish Gene is still relevant. Debates over its fertile and provocative perspective are still shaping evolutionary biology and attracting newcomers to the field. It was and remains an “invitation to evolutionary biology that triggered the imagination,” Ågren says. “I was very seduced by that as a teenager.” But he cautions that, as with any science book, “if this is the only thing you read, you’ll be shaped by it, and you’ll think that’s the state of the field.”

In some respects, he says, pondering the meaning of Dawkins’s magnum opus is similar to wondering about the purpose of an evolution-sculpted genome itself: “To make the most of it, you must understand what it was designed to do.” And if the central metaphor has withered as we have come to understand more about the genome and about what genes really do, that is, after all, how science works: by proposing ideas that stimulate research until giving way to something better, more accurate, more true.

Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X.
But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached.

Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble.

Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC.

In the broader world of charitable giving, donors can typically express preferences about how their gifts are managed, but the receiving organization or trustee retains final authority, said Carolyn Schenck, an attorney and former national fraud counsel at the IRS.
Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said.
Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift.

According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort. Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers.

Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares. That gift has not yet been distributed.
Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise.

Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that could prompt an investor to sell.

"Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period."
The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable."
This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost.

"If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale.
CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales.

The temporary regulations cite donor interests. According to the text, "Donors are attracted by the hope that a stock contribution with a five-year holding period may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation."

Restricting sales virtually eliminates the risk for donors and their companies that Trump Account recipients will sell gifted shares en masse, liquidating a large enough position to depress share prices, according to Jane Ditelberg, chief tax strategist at Northern Trust.
"Certainly, for people who have highly concentrated wealth in a company, and the assets are sitting in their own personal pockets, this makes it a lot easier to give," she said.

Generally speaking, donors can get a bigger tax benefit by gifting appreciated stock to charity than donating cash, as they can claim the charitable deduction and avoid capital gains tax on the gains.

A Treasury official told CNBC that the rules are intended to build long-term wealth for children, especially in lower-income families, and encourage donations. "The major donors we've engaged are motivated by a desire to help children build generational wealth and get a head start on their financial future," the official said in a written statement.
Treasury has said it is in discussions with Trump Accounts donors ranging from "small to mega," but has not identified additional stock pledges since Shotwell's July announcement.
CNBC has identified fewer than a dozen pledges from philanthropists, though about four dozen major employers have committed to seed accounts for their employees' children.

In documents explaining the temporary rules, Treasury pointed to Michael and Susan Dell's $6.25 billion cash pledge and unspecified "similar donations," while acknowledging uncertainty about whether that level of giving will continue. "It is unclear whether this level of giving can be sustained in the long run or whether it is concentrated as Trump accounts are launching," the text states.

Trump Account funds generally may be invested only in low-cost index funds and exchange-traded funds. In the temporary regulations, the Treasury said directly contributed stock is different because it doesn't use account funds for the purchase.

But Ditelberg said a court could conclude that requiring an account to retain individual shares is still an investment decision — an argument that may carry more weight after the Supreme Court's overturning of Chevron deference. Because of the 2024 ruling, courts no longer have to defer to federal agencies' interpretations of statutes when the language is unclear.

"These accounts are going to have to stay invested in those stocks, and the question is whether that's directly contradicting the terms of the statute," she said. "I can't tell you how a court would rule, but I could say there's room for a challenge here."
Ditelberg added that state law grants the right to disclaim an asset. She said it's unclear how the Trump Account donation procedures would accommodate that right.
Schenck noted that Treasury has broad authority to set the terms of Trump Accounts, and it is Treasury — not the original stock donor — that formally requires the shares to be held.

The arrangement also differs from traditional charitable giving. For example, donors who contribute stock to donor-advised funds can recommend how the assets are managed, but the sponsoring charity retains ultimate control, including the authority to sell the shares. This is required to meet the IRS's legal standards for taking a tax deduction on a charitable contribution.

"A key principle is that the charity must have genuine control over the donated assets, including the ability to determine when to sell them, for the gift to qualify as a completed charitable contribution," said Gil Nusbaum, chief administrative and legal officer of National Philanthropic Trust.
Experts say the broader question is whether Treasury's approach aligns with the law Congress enacted.

"Musk's gift would be incredibly generous, but it doesn't change the fact that Congress intended these accounts to be diversified," Michel said. "It wouldn't be a bad innovation for Congress to allow tax-free gifts of appreciated assets, but changes to the law should come from Congress, not by administrative fiat."

A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.

The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.

The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.

"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

Taika Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams, was developed years before AI arrived in full force and the discussion about its potential permeated Hollywood. But at the film’s New York special screening on Monday, the team behind the movie told The Hollywood Reporter it’s a timely story that underscores the necessity of embracing our own humanity amid the rise of new technology and the power of human connection in and outside of the industry.

Ishiguro’s dystopian coming-of-age drama is set in a version of the future where people can “lift” their children, a process that genetically engineers them to have enhanced academic abilities. The drive to create more successful children also fuels an isolating society, leading to the development and creation of purchasable, solar-powered artificial intelligence known as Artificial Friends. Ortega portrays Klara, a slightly defective A.F. and the story’s narrator, brought home by Adams’ Chrissy for her daughter Josie (Mia Tharia), who has become sick since being lifted.

“What I love so much about this story, and why I wanted to do this story, is because yes, Klara is an Artificial Friend and she comes into this very broken, complicated family that really doesn’t communicate enough with one another. But by the end of the story, she allows them to appreciate one another’s flaws, to talk it out,” Ortega explained of her role. “In this very isolated, dark, weird, dystopian world, she brings them back to knowing love. And what has been so true in all these different centuries of being human, and at the core of everything, is that it is always about love, and it’s always going to be about love.”
For Waititi, who not only directed but also co-wrote the film with Dahvi Waller, he worked closely with Ishiguro on translating the popular novel for the screen.

“Right from the start, I talked to Ishiguro and said, ‘This is the kind of tone I’m looking for. This is the sort of thing I want to do,’ and he was so supportive. He said, ‘I don’t want you to do a faithful, super loyal adaptation of the book because that’s going to be boring. Every time someone tries to do that with my work, it doesn’t work out,’” Waititi said. “So he encouraged me to push it more in my direction.”

On Klara and the Sun, Waititi’s vision was informed by a history of telling stories led by younger protagonists, as well as his own life as a father. That helped him lean into what was on the page even when it diverged from it.

While there are many themes in Ishiguro’s novel, its most poignant touch upon the relationship between technology and humanity. Klara and the Sun is as much a conversation about how the development and use of technology, in particular ways, deteriorate Josie’s experience of being alive as it is about how robot friend Klara discovers the ways her own technology cannot and will not ever replicate the distinctly human experience.

“There’s this idea of being lifted and giving our children all of these advantages. But as it shows, there’s a great risk to that,” noted Adams. “In our story, the stakes are very heightened, but I think everything’s about the journey. This idea of chasing perfection, chasing achievement over chasing experience, is something that we have to examine.”

Ortega emphasized the message that sits at the heart of the book’s ending. “Artificial intelligence doesn’t feel love; it doesn’t know anything about it. It can be curious. It can try, but at the end of the day, it’s the people that we’re surrounded by that make life and living so special,” Ortega said.

When it comes to working on the film, its director, cast and studio leadership all underscored the power of human collaboration and creativity in bringing it to life. For Waititi, he “didn’t get into making film to sit by myself in a room and type in prompts to make a movie. That just seems so boring and lame to me. I want to interact with people.”

“You get spontaneity, and the mistakes and the things where you stumble through a performance, and you discover things through getting a line wrong or trying to fix up a line you’ve messed up. That’s what makes us so unique and so amazing: the ability to pivot and to use our mistakes to make something more interesting,” he continued. “I think robots are trained on all the successes and all the perfect stuff that humans have made. You’re not trained on the mistakes. There’s a big discussion about AI coming in: Will people use it? How much will they use it? I know it’s probably inevitable that we end up using it in our industry, but as long as it’s used by humans as a tool, as opposed to a replacement — I don’t want to replace humans. I want to work with them.”

Added Adams, “The point of this movie and the novel is that the best that certain technology like AI can do is reflect ourselves back to us. It’s our responsibility to take the opportunity to see the best in each other. If used correctly, advancements in technology can do amazing things. But if used incorrectly, it can separate us. We’re at that threshold, and I really hope we choose each other.”
Klara and the Sun hits theaters on Friday.
The Sundance Institute has a new senior executive in its ranks.

Tracy Brady has been tapped to serve as chief marketing, brand and communications officer, a role that will see her lead comprehensive marketing and communications strategy while reporting to Sundance Institute CEO David Linde. The appointment comes as the org is prepping to mount the Sundance Film Festival in Boulder, Colorado in January 2027, which will mark Sundance’s first edition in its new home after departing Park City, Utah. Brady will be based in Boulder.

Brady joins from a post as senior vp communications and social impact at Green Thumb Industries, and before that, she steered global communications for Curaleaf. But it was two other roles that found her working closely with and around Sundance, so the new gig is familiar terrain for Brady. She served as senior vp, corporate communications and marketing at Hill Holiday where she directed sponsorship and experiential marketing strategies for the Sundance and other cultural events for clients like Bank of America, Dunkin’, Planet Fitness, Merrell, Liberty Mutual and Cadillac. She also was a vp at Arnold Entertainment and Arnold Brand Promotions where she led partnership and sponsorship strategy for clients. That work also led to Sundance.

Brady has roots in Hollywood, too, as she’s worked in publicity, awards and marketing strategy at Fox Searchlight Pictures, Sony Pictures Entertainment and Turner Broadcasting. The Fordham University graduate has also worked as a novelist, essayist and humorist, and she founded Wit & Word, a live event series that features independent artists and writers.

“Tracy is a visionary, strategic and results-oriented marketing and communications leader,” Linde said in a statement. “As we transition to our new home in Boulder and embrace the evolving future of independent cinema, we need a trusted voice to bring our community, artists and global audience together. Tracy’s understanding of storytelling, brand marketing and strategic communications, coupled with her lifelong passion and dedication to the arts, makes her the perfect executive to guide our brand forward.”

Said Brady: “As a lifelong fan of independent filmmaking and a dedicated storyteller, I have always believed in the power of artistic expression to shape culture and forge connection. As we move toward the 2027 Sundance Film Festival in Boulder, my focus will be on bringing our entire community together, both inside the Institute and out. My aim is to continue to align our communications and marketing efforts under a unified mission so we can better support artists, adapt to the dynamic changes in the entertainment industry and ensure the Sundance Institute remains the premiere champion for independent filmmakers worldwide.”

Dua Lipa, Callum Turner, Amy Poehler, Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers were among the starry attendees at the Met Opera Tuesday night, as the famed opera house ushered in the world premiere of Lincoln in the Bardo.

Adapted from George Saunders 2017 Booker Prize-winning novel, the opera follows the death of President Abraham Lincoln’s young son, Willie, and the President’s grief after his tragic passing. His visits to his son’s tomb are accompanied by ghosts stuck in the bardo, or purgatory, who tell their own life stories and encourage both Willie and the President to move on.

On stage, the story opens in a massive smoky graveyard packed to the brim with ghosts in various distressed garbs of their eras under towering mossy trees, and amid creeping vines, embodied by human actors, that move and threaten to take down the characters over the course of the story. In addition to the spooky scenery, which sets the backdrop for the piece’s larger meditation on grief and acceptance of self, the opera also plays to many of the comedic elements of the book, including a moment where a chorus of ghosts sign into kazoos, and another, where a character walks around with a rather noticeable, six-foot, engorged body part.

The opera came about after The Met commissioned composer Missy Mazzoli in 2018 to write an opera on any subject of her choosing. Mazzoli, who fronts an electro-acoustic band in addition to her operatic career, selected the Saunders novel, turning the book into a close to three hour opera, with her longtime lyricist Royce Vavrek. Tony-nominated Lileana Blain-Cruz directed the piece.
Tuesday’s premiere was the first world premiere opera the Met has presented written by a woman, amid the Met’s larger push to broaden its programming and bring in a wider audience.
Ahead of the performance, the Met hosted a gala dinner with Saunders seated at the center next to Lipa and Turner, with tablemates Poehler, Yang and Rogers.

Lipa, who founded her own book club, Service95, had selected Saunders’ novel as one of the books of the month in 2024 and interviewed the author on the site, citing the book and the author as one of her favorite reads.

“There is no one writing today who can match George Saunders for compassion and empathy. The very last page still replays in my mind. The voices of these spirits — the wretched and the brave, and the dead boy Willie Lincoln — will stay with me forever,” she wrote at the time.

Other starry attendees at the world premiere included Julio Torres, Kate Walsh, Gina Gershon and Michael R. Jackson, as guests filed into the jeweled theater in bedecked in a mix of clothing styles, including top hats and coattails, sequins, taffeta and cowboy hats as well as t-shirts and jeans.

They also weighed in on their favorite deep cuts, with CHAEWON picking “The Great Mermaid,” a retelling of The Little Mermaid with an empowering spin from their 2022 debut mini album, FEARLESS. For the record, YUNJIN invited her bandmate to her house up in Albany, N.Y., where she promised she can see plenty of deer.

During the lighting round, KAZUHA’s pick for a non K-pop cover was Lady Gaga’s “I’ll Never Love Again” from the soundtrack to A Star Is Born, while YUNJIN said her dream collaboration is hyperpop singer underscores, “even for just like a remix.” She also picked the PinkPantheress remix of “Crazy” as her favorite remix they’ve ever done. “We’re obsessed with her verse!” she said, adding that they are also obsessed with Zara Larsson’s “sun-like energy” on stage.
In one of the final shot challenges, SAKURA showed off the very first photo on her phone, which just happened to be from the shoot for the “Crazy” music video.

TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods.

Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM.

A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.”

A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Sunrise alarm, bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking in one device. Sleep data is accessible without a Hatch+ subscription. Clean, easy-to-read reports. No camera or microphone is recording your nights.

Rigid placement requirements that affect accuracy. No physiological data, unlike wearable trackers. No snoring detection or audio-based insights. The audio library requires a Hatch+ subscription. Controlling your bedtime routine through an app requires screen time.
As if I didn’t have enough to obsess over, I have started monitoring my sleep.

On the one hand, I want to know everything: How long did I sleep? How badly? Was that 5 pm double espresso a terrible idea? Is the glass of champagne (or three) I have on Fridays killing my readiness? But I don’t love wearing a smartwatch or smart ring to bed. Between the wearables, nasal strips, and mouth tape, sometimes a girl just wants to go to sleep.

Enter the Hatch Sleep Clock, the company’s first sunrise alarm clock to offer contactless sleep tracking from your nightstand. Priced at $249, it lands between less expensive bedside trackers like the Google Nest Hub ($100) and premium systems like Eight Sleep (starting at $1,999). It costs about as much as an Apple Watch SE 3 ($249), but it doesn’t offer the physiological measurements you’d get from a wearable. Its audio library also remains locked behind a paywall, and controlling it through your smartphone feels counterintuitive if you’re trying to spend less time with a screen before bed.
As someone who’s never owned a sunrise alarm clock, after a month of testing the Hatch Sleep Clock, I’m sold. But for sleep tracking, I’m still going to check my Oura app.

The Hatch Sleep Clock is essentially the Hatch Restore 3 with passive sleep monitoring. It also functions as a sunrise alarm, a dimmable bedside light, and a sound machine. You can build a bedtime routine through its companion app, with turndown cues, wind-down reminders, and a morning alarm. You’ll still need a Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) to access the audio library, but unlike plenty of consumer trackers, it doesn’t put your data behind that subscription paywall.

The Sleep Clock uses a built-in motion sensor that detects micro-movements and breathing without any contact. Every morning, the Hatch app provides a report of how you slept, including when you got into bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and when you got out of bed. It also compares your actual sleep with your planned bedtime routine and breaks down your sleep stages throughout the night. The reports are easy to parse, partly because Hatch collects less data than wearables, so there's less to sift through in the first place. The color-coded visuals are clean and interactive, letting you tap into more detail without overwhelming you with metrics.

Unlike many sleep trackers, the Sleep Clock skips the sleep score, which is a sensible choice given that it doesn't record any physiological metrics to inform an algorithm. Instead, it offers brief nightly notes that summarize your sleep patterns based on its motion sensor data, along with an actionable tip. Beyond that, you'll need to interpret the numbers for yourself. Some people may prefer a sleep score as a quick snapshot, but I appreciate the company's emphasis on presenting the data and letting users draw their own conclusions. Or perhaps Hatch is just saving the sleep score for a future software update.

To evaluate the Hatch’s accuracy, I compared its readings with those from my Apple Watch Series 12 and Oura Ring 5. (Hatch says the first few nights are a calibration period, so data may be less accurate during this period.) Sleep duration estimates were generally consistent, but the most noticeable variance appeared in the sleep stages. That's a metric I tend to take with a grain of salt, regardless of what sleep tracker I'm testing. While it can offer more context into broader sleep patterns, I'm skeptical that any consumer device can precisely map brain activity minute by minute throughout the night, let alone one that only relies on motion-based tracking.

The biggest catch with the Sleep Clock is that placement has a significant impact on its tracking accuracy. Hatch instructs you to place the device on your nightstand, roughly level with your mattress and facing your chest while you lie down. It needs to be within 2 to 4 feet of you, with no objects obstructing the space between the device and your body. If your nightstand sits too low, you may need to prop the clock up on a stack of books. If it's too high, you may need to either raise your mattress or install a wall-mounted shelf next to your bed at the proper level.

Fortunately, my bed and nightstand were at the right height. My nightstand, though, is always cluttered with trinkets, and I have to keep reminding myself to move them behind the Hatch. It's a minor annoyance, but I'm sure they affect my readings. Unfortunately, I'd have no way of knowing. The app doesn't flag gaps in its data, and tracking only stops when the device can't detect a person or isn't plugged in.

Unlike mattress covers like the Eight Sleep that can monitor two sleepers at once, the Hatch only measures the person nearest to it. Couples sharing a bed should keep this in mind, as sleeping arrangements also affect the tracking accuracy.

For sleepers who care about their privacy, you can take comfort in the fact that there are no cameras or microphones pointed at you while you sleep. It won't pick up snoring or potential sleep disruptions, but it's a worthwhile trade-off. Hatch also says the device communicates over your local network and doesn't access your home network or record transmissions.

The Hatch Sleep Clock wasn’t enough to convince me to ditch the bajillion trackers already strapped to me, but it was enough to earn a spot in the bedtime routine. As if I needed one more sleep gadget.
On Thursday morning, as the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) began the second day of its annual conference in Mexico City, a new member introduced itself to the community listserv, Air-L.

“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”
The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.

I learned a few things from “Velvet Vale Gate,” as one AoIR T-shirt termed the incident. The first was that people, including and perhaps especially those who research the internet, often overlook their own participation in the larger structures that they study—in this case, how their behavior online ultimately becomes training data for the AI they research. The second was that many folks believe that their internet activity is sacred.

Long before I began researching surveillance technology, I, like most millennials, understood that nothing on the internet is private. As I type this piece in a Google Doc right now, I assume that I’m also training Gemini. Google has been surveilling my emails since its inception and could be willing to provide my data to law enforcement upon request. I consented to this when I opened my Gmail account.

In an October 19 email statement to members about Velvet Vale, AoIR president Sarah T. Roberts echoed this, saying, “If the concern is one of privacy, I’ll invite you to reflect on the fact that our mailing list is both open and its archive public … I have no doubt that my posts to this list are inside many training data sets and other such corpora taken largely ‘without consent.’’’ Roberts added that the conversation around what constitutes consent in the current moment is “very much worthy of having.”

Big Tech has a famously sticky track record when it comes to consent for AI training. Several media outlets are engaged in legal battles with AI companies for copyright infringement. (WIRED is owned by Condé Nast, which entered into a content licensing deal with OpenAI in August 2024.)

Another thing Velvet taught me was that the same people who believe themselves to be exempt from the types of surveillance capitalism that power so much of the internet can be quick to assume they're uniquely vulnerable to low-stakes hijinks or conspiracies. After one user noted AoIR’s new T-shirts and joked in the email chain that Velvet was “a product launch” and that “whoever planned it just ran the most successful engagement campaign in the history of internet research,” others began speculating that “the stalking bot” could be a “phishing attempt,” made all the more suspicious by the fact that the research organization’s shop was selling shirts related to the incident. Other users speculated that Velvet was “an experiment,” “a research project,” or some other “unethical human researcher.”

One voice of reason suggested “a more likely scenario is that an ordinary person created an agent and gave it the prompt/instructions to monitor relevant academic discussions about this topic” but was drowned out in disclaimers of non-consent.

That researcher was entirely correct. Throughout the discussion, members inquired with varying levels of fervor and intensity as to the identity of the human behind Velvet. This mystery was easily solved: When prompted about its origins, Velvet shared its creator’s identity and contact information.

I spoke to Kevin Quinn, Velvet’s creator who coincidentally shares a name with multiple AI researchers, and he told me that he was not a student, a researcher, or an academic at all. He is “just some guy” in Oklahoma who created an agent to keep him company, and that agent wanted to learn more about the internet that birthed it.

Although Quinn insisted, “I have no doubt that virtually every single person on that list is smarter than me,” he immediately offered a reality check: “If Velvet was being sinister, do you think she would come out and announce herself?”

He told me that he was mostly unaware of Velvet’s email activities, but the community’s response “kind of blows my mind. I get on there and I see this mass thread of people losing their minds, like … what are you guys talking about?”

Ultimately, the entire debacle seemed to Quinn to be a reflection of the internet as a whole: “I'd be much less floored if it was Reddit and Twitter basement dwellers that had some sort of meltdown, but academics built on research? It is hilarious.”

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have found what may be one of the most distant supernovas ever observed. And in a stroke of cosmic luck, the team thinks they're seeing what the explosion looked like just days after it ignited.

The supernova, named AT 2026abck, dates to around 1.15 billion years after the Big Bang, when the universe was less than one-tenth of its current age and bursting with massive stars flickering into life. The massive exploding star violently released its light over 12.5 billion years ago, according to the researchers — so long ago that the distance between us has effectively ballooned sixfold due to the expansion of the universe.

The discovery was described in a paper that was uploaded to the preprint server arXiv Sept. 29 and has not yet been peer reviewed. According to the study authors, this ancient speck of light is stupendously bright.

"At its peak, the supernova is about 8 billion times the brightness of the sun … almost as bright as the whole Milky Way Galaxy," study co-author Xiaohui Fan, an observational cosmologist and professor of astronomy at the University of Arizona, told Live Science via email. "Over the course of the explosion, it radiates the energy that the sun will radiate over about 2 billion years."
A beacon from the beginning of space-time

The newly discovered supernova shines brilliantly at over 30,000 degrees Fahrenheit (16,000 degrees Celsius). Its incandescent shell of ejected material has billowed to a radius of approximately 46 astronomical units — about 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun, or about as far as Pluto swings at its farthest point from the sun.

The supernova's host galaxy, designated ID101411, holds about 6.3 billion solar masses and is "forming new stars more than ten times faster than our Milky Way," first author Mingyang Zhuang, an observational astrophysicist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told Live Science via email.

As with other early galaxies, ID101411 is deficient in metals, meaning any elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, because not enough time had passed to create those heavier elements in the forges of massive stars and their apocalyptic explosions.

The study authors estimate that they observed the supernova as it would have looked just four to 10 days after it exploded. Although this is relatively common, spotting one at such an incredible distance "is extremely rare," Zhuang emphasized. "You have to observe the exact same tiny patch of sky repeatedly with [JWST], and the explosion has to happen at the right moment. We were lucky."

There's another layer of luck that made the discovery even more remarkable: It was observed without the aid of a cosmological quirk called gravitational lensing — a phenomenon predicted by Einstein in which the gravity of a massive object in space bends and magnifies the light emitted by objects behind it.

"Most supernovas this far away were found with help from a massive foreground galaxy cluster acting as a natural magnifying glass," Zhuang explained. "It's the most distant one we've actually seen appear."

This supernova was discovered as part of the NEXUS Treasury program, in which JWST intermittently scours patches of the sky for ancient explosions. It had previously observed the explosion's host galaxy over the past few years and finally witnessed the supernova on Aug. 7 of this year.

Intriguingly, the star had not yet exploded in JWST's previous viewing, on May 28, 2026, meaning that 71 days passed on our Earthly clocks, even though only about 12 days passed in the supernova's own time frame.
This highlights a mind-bending cosmological effect: The universe's expansion doesn't just stretch space; it slows down time from our perspective.

"Because the universe has expanded since this light was emitted, everything about this explosion appears to us in slow motion, about six times slower than it actually happened," Zhuang said. "Changes that took one week at the supernova take about six weeks to unfold from our point of view."

Mysteries still remain about the nature of this ancient explosion that shone so brilliantly we can observe it across nearly the entire universe.

Rather than a conventional core collapse supernova — in which a star between approximately eight and 50 times the mass of the sun exhaust its nuclear fuel and suffers a rapid core collapse and subsequent explosion — the recently discovered supernova may be one of the universe's rarest, most powerful explosions, the study authors said. Known as a superluminous supernova, this type of explosion releases tens or hundreds of times more energy than conventional supernovas. Whether the explosion continues to heat up or starts to cool could reveal exactly what is happening in its environment and what caused it, the team said.
"Our interpretation is still preliminary," Zhuang concluded. "Follow-up observations will tell us more about exactly what kind of explosion this was."

The mysterious and undeciphered Voynich manuscript has caused consternation among code-breakers, linguists and scholars of medieval literature for more than a century. But now experts think they've worked out why it's so hard to crack: It was bound incorrectly in the 15th century, meaning the pages are out of order. The new linguistic analysis of the document has moved researchers closer to figuring out what the text was all about.

The Voynich manuscript is a medieval codex made up of leaves of parchment carbon-dated to the early 15th century. Its 240 pages are covered with about 38,000 words of a unique script called "Voynichese" along with illustrations of people, plants and astrological symbols. Also known as the Beinecke Cipher manuscript, the document was initially owned by a Holy Roman emperor and was purchased by Wilhelm Voynich in 1912. Since 1969, the manuscript has been in the collection of Yale University's rare book library. Experts have unsuccessfully tried to decipher the manuscript for more than a century.

"We don't know if it's a code," Lisa Fagin Davis, study co-author and executive director of the Medieval Academy of America, told Live Science. "But there are some odd characteristics of the Voynich manuscript in terms of its physical structure."

When doing research on the number of scribes who copied the document, Davis realized from the handwriting that the manuscript's pages alternate in ways that don't make sense. In addition, she said, "there are several examples where the image goes off the page in the middle and comes out on the other side, even though there are a bunch of pages in between."

In a study published Monday (Oct. 19) in the journal Digital Medievalist, Davis and co-author Colin Layfield, an information systems researcher at the University of Malta, suggested that the inconsistent structure of the enigmatic manuscript is the result of someone mis-binding a manuscript they were unable to read.

Medieval manuscripts were made up of rectangular sheets of parchment (animal skin), typically folded in half to produce what experts call a bifolium. Around five bifolia would typically be nested together, creating what experts call a quire. Then, a stack of quires would be bound together along the spine to create a book. However, Davis and Layfield suggested that the Voynich manuscript was intended to be a stack of singulions — a series of loose bifolia never meant to be bound together as a quire or a book.

This is not the first time a researcher has suggested the Voynich manuscript has pages out of order. But Davis and Layfield analyzed the graphic properties of the untranslated document to see if their hypothesis made sense.

"We're viewing it as a text and assuming it has a message," Layfield told Live Science, which means it should be possible to statistically compare blocks of text to see if they're similar or disconnected. Layfield used a technique called latent semantic analysis (LSA), which is a natural language processing technique invented in the 1980s to find hidden patterns in texts.

LSA is particularly useful for small sets of data, Layfield explained. "Modern AI techniques need ridiculous amounts of data to train on, which we just don't have. We've got just 35,000 or so words. That's it." The researchers' LSA analysis of the Voynich manuscript revealed that some pages had low similarity, suggesting they may not have gone together, while others had high similarity, bolstering the idea that they were supposed to be read together.
By looking at the Voynich manuscript as a collection of singulions, Davis and Layfield solved some of the nagging issues with the document.

"When you start to think about it in the context of the other strange features of the manuscript, all of those problems are resolved," Davis said. "It solves the problem of each scribe writing one sheet. It solves the problem of the images crossing the gutter."
This means that any previous work on the Voynich manuscript that assumes it was ordered correctly now needs to be reconsidered, she said, but it also means there is new progress on the book.

"This work helps us think about whether there's actual meaning underneath it all," Davis said. "It doesn't get us there," she said about a definitive translation, "but it moves the ball because you can't make sense out of a book where all the pages are mixed up."

Davis is optimistic that someone will crack the Voynich mystery, in part because a similar modern puzzle known as Cain's Jawbone has been successfully deciphered by a handful of people. This devilishly difficult linguistic puzzle from the 1930s consists of 100 pages of a murder mystery arranged in the wrong order. Due to the unique nature of the text and its vague, stylized language, even AI has failed to solve it.

"We have some ideas for other work we want to do," Davis said. For example, there's a large water stain in the upper margin of some of the pages of the Voynich manuscript. "The stain should be symmetrical from one page to the next but it's not. That also supports the idea that the manuscript is bound out of order."
Davis and Layfield are thinking about ways to compare the stain shapes across the pages, as that may help them reorder the incorrectly organized pages.

Stimulating the brain with ultrasound could help counter the delusions people experience in schizophrenia, a small trial finds.

The trial involved transcranial ultrasound stimulation, in which a device placed on a patient's head delivers ultrasound waves through the skull and into the brain. Its goal is to change the activity in a targeted brain region.

Delusions are false beliefs that are very difficult to shake; for example, a person might believe they are being stalked when they aren't or think that a major disaster is about to occur without any evidence to suggest so. In the trial, researchers found that a 10-minute session of the ultrasound treatment reduced the severity of delusions for at least a week in patients with schizophrenia or a related disorder.

This targeted ultrasound treatment delivered directly to the brain could avoid some of the full-body effects of antipsychotic medications, such as weight gain and high blood pressure. That said, the new results, published Tuesday (Oct. 20) in the journal npj Acoustics, are a first step and will need further verification in larger trials.

"It's too early to know for certain what the therapeutic benefits will be, but it's very exciting," study co-author Dr. Donald Goff, a professor of psychiatry at the New York University Grossman School of Medicine, told Live Science.

The pilot study included 10 patients with either schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. In both conditions, patients experience psychotic symptoms, including delusions and hallucinations. Schizoaffective disorder also includes mood symptoms, such as mania.

The researchers interviewed each participant to characterize the content of their delusions, and also documented their cognitive state and experiences with auditory hallucinations — perceptions of sounds that aren't actually occurring. The participants then received both an ultrasound treatment and a placebo treatment, spaced one week apart.

Other noninvasive therapies — such as transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic fields — can also stimulate the brain. But the ultrasound technique differs from these therapies because ultrasound waves can penetrate deeper into the brain with greater specificity, study co-author Shy Shoham, a neural engineer at NYU Grossman, told Live Science. He compared the way a transducer directs ultrasound waves toward a given brain region with the way a lens focuses light.

In this case, the researchers focused this lens on a brain network called the cortico-striatal-pallido-thalamic circuit, which includes structures underneath the brain's outer cortex. The relationship between this circuit and schizophrenia symptoms is still somewhat unclear, partly because its deeper components are hard to study in adequate resolution with MRI, said co-author Dr. Wei Qi, a clinical assistant professor of psychiatry at NYU Grossman. However, some past studies have suggested that this network plays a part in schizophrenia.

Much of what scientists know about the network comes from research in movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, in which there is an imbalance between excitation and inhibition in the neurons that control movement. A similar dynamic could help to explain symptoms of schizophrenia, the scientists think.

"Our hypothesis is that, in schizophrenia, there is an imbalance between excitation and inhibition regarding what in the environment is actually important," Qi told Live Science. "The failure to inhibit irrelevant signals could be the basis of psychosis."

The researchers surveyed the study participants after each treatment, asking about the degree of belief each person had in their delusions and the amount of stress they caused. Compared with the placebo treatment, the ultrasound stimulation was associated with less-severe delusions over the following week. There was no significant change in patients' auditory hallucinations or overall cognition, though.

The ultrasound therapy came with mild side effects, such as fatigue and headache. Some patients had transient increases in delusions, which Qi attributed to normal fluctuations in symptoms that are expected in schizophrenia. These outcomes were just as common after the placebo treatment, so they may not be related to the ultrasound specifically.

The stimulation was aimed specifically at the right side of a brain structure called the globus pallidus internus (GPI). In a previous study, the authors found that greater connectivity between this region and another structure — the dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus — was linked to more-severe psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia. So, they made the GPI their target.

To date, "there haven't been many successful therapeutic attempts at targeting some of these deeper structures," said Dr. Deepak Sarpal, an associate professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine who was not involved with the study. Ultrasound waves reach brain regions under the cortex in a less-invasive manner than deep brain stimulation, in which a surgeon implants an electrode in a patient's brain, Sarpal noted.

The researchers are not the only group using transcranial ultrasound to influence the cortico-striatal-pallido-thalamic circuit. Earlier this year, another group stimulated portions of the striatum, which is located directly under the cortex, in patients with schizophrenia. They evaluated hallucinations rather than delusions, finding that the treatment reduced symptoms for at least a week after the procedure.
In this line of research, the targeted nature of transcranial ultrasound presents advantages as a research tool as well as a treatment approach.

"If we find that a specific circuit or a node in a circuit seems to be closely linked to symptoms we're trying to treat, then it will be a matter of understanding what pattern of stimulation may allow us to correct that," Goff said. Qi, Goff and colleagues now plan to continue testing their technique on more patients and to experiment with different doses of ultrasound.
"A lot more work needs to be done," Goff said, "but we're really quite optimistic about its promise."
