Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.

While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.

The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.

French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.

Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.

French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.

That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and their continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.

Defence ball launchers, for example, fire rubber projectiles at 185mph (300kph). The explosive grenades that injured gilets jaunes protesters in the late 2010s and killed an environmental protester in 2014 have been phased out, but been replaced by pyrotechnic stun grenades.

Designed to disperse crowds through both impact and a 160dB acoustic shock, these have caused multiple injuries in recent years, including lost eyes and teeth, fractured jaws and several amputated limbs. They also frequently instil mass panic.

Violent policing methods are also fostered by France’s almost unique culture of street protest. A legacy of insurrection dating back to the 1789 revolution means protesters know the street can, and generally does, force governments to back down.

Unlike in Germany or the Netherlands, French unions, while they may strike often, are not formal government negotiating partners. The top-heavy, presidential structure of the Fifth Republic marginalises institutional consultation.

That means a heavily centralised state often passes laws with little popular agreement, making the “power of the street” one of citizens’ few viable means of forcing concessions. Protest here is regarded as a civic duty and a legitimate democratic tool.

That creates a vicious circle. French authorities see large crowds as an existential threat, so send in the police. Their military-style tactics entrench the aggression and alienate peaceful demonstrators. This prompts the more radical groups to opt for more violent tactics. But rather than isolating those elements, police respond with baton charges and munitions. And that turns protests into battles.

Data from conflict monitoring organisations, such as Acled, consistently shows that France, perhaps surprisingly, does not always record western Europe’s highest number of demonstrations (Germany and Italy also vie for that title).

But it does show that France consistently records the highest rates of escalated, high-intensity unrest, including street barricades, widespread vandalism and looting, arson attacks and direct confrontations between protesters and police.

France’s approach to policing and crowd management has for decades drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors and civil society groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Council of Europe.

Reports have documented instances of excessive force, misuse of grenades and rubber bullets, arbitrary mass arrests and routine teargas deployment against largely non-violent protesters. But the model persists, and is even expanding.

Last month, thousands marched in protest at a proposed “licence to kill” law seeking to establish a legal “presumption of self-defence” for police officers and gendarmes using firearms in the line of duty.

The law, opposed by civil rights groups, leftwing politicians, the magistrates’ union and the UN, would in effect shift the burden of proof on to victims and their families to demonstrate that a police shooting was disproportionate.

In essence, critics argue, it would institutionalise police impunity; reinforcing, once more, a security culture that treats public dissent and social tension not as democratic realities to be managed, but as insurrections to be repressed. The battle for France’s streets is far from over.

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin the process of independence, delivering a decisive victory for supporters of Canadian unity and deepening divisions within the separatist movement.
With nearly 1.9m votes counted, roughly 76% people supported remaining in Canada, while 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, celebrated the result.
“Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.
The results showed an overwhelming majority of Albertans had voted to remain and one radio show host posted: “Someone owes Albertans $130m for this theatrical waste of taxpayers’ money.”
Pollster David Coletto told the Guardian that residents felt the referendum was “a distraction away” from what they wanted their government to focus on.

“There was almost a general sadness about the wasted energy spent on this rather than the more real threats they see, including the Trump administration,” he said. “Most Albertans feel deep grievances with the federal government while also being proudly Canadian. The marriage may be rocky at times, and most Albertans want to see some thing changed, but very few are willing to see the marriage end.”

The province’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Others took a different view of the results. “The result is bleak. Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat, however, it changes nothing about the reality of the circumstances Albertans find themselves in,” David Parker, a longtime far-right organiser linked to a massive breach of voter information, wrote on social media.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a by-election.

Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence. And in the aftermath of the results, one prominent separatist leader said he would push for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.

Jeffrey Rath told Global News that the Alberta independence will remain nothing but a dream long as Smith, whom he called an “avowed federalist” remains in power. He said it was time for separatists to “take back ownership” of the UCP.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

"The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revisited her widely-discussed 2024 question to former Vice President Kamala Harris during an event on Monday, calling the former Democratic presidential nominee's answer and refusal to distance herself from former President Joe Biden at the time "problematic."

Brian Teta, the talk show's executive producer and host of its "Behind the Table" podcast, selected the moment as Hostin's most memorable on the show. He said it was a "seminal moment" in the 2024 election cycle.

Hostin described the question as a "gift" and said she thought Harris would have to distance herself from Biden because of his approval ratings at the time. She also said "The View" was the perfect venue to ask the question, calling the liberal show's audience "her people."

"I actually thought the answer was going to be, you know, ‘We had a lot of wins in this administration. I was there for those wins, but I, as a woman of color, as a child of immigrants, as I have a different lived experience, and I intend to bring that lived experience with me into the White House. I will do this. I will do that. I will do this. I will do that. I will do that.’ That was what I was expecting. I was not expecting, 'Not a single thing comes to mind.' And I knew honestly when she said it that it was really problematic," Hostin said.
The co-hosts noted that the moment was discussed in books published after the 2024 election, including Harris' memoir, "107 Days," and was also featured in a political ad for President Donald Trump.
In "107 Days," Harris wrote that she had no idea she had just "pulled the pin on a hand grenade," with her answer to Hostin's question. She wrote that her staff was beside themselves.

"Stationed at various places around the set, my staff were beside themselves. Political operatives have an eye to see a moment, and I could kick myself for giving the other side that moment. During the commercial break, while I was having a bit of fun with some young students I’d noticed in the audience who were obviously playing hooky, offering to write notes to their teachers after the show, Opal [Vadhan] passed me a note from our team, telling me to return to that question and mention that a big difference would be that I would put a Republican in my cabinet," she wrote in her book.
Teta and the co-hosts said they all knew her response was going to be a problem.
Co-host Ana Navarro said Harris' staff "ran" because staff members knew immediately that Harris needed to return to the question and address her answer.
During the show on Friday, both Navarro and Haines said they wouldn't tell Harris not to run, but questioned if she would be the best option for the Democratic Party.

"If the Democrats want to win, I don't think she's the right candidate because I think the Democrats have been screaming for new energy. They've been saying we need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot. From the first time when she didn't ... she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time. People are clamoring for fresh energy, and there's a lot of candidates," Haines said.

Co-host Joy Behar has said on several occasions that she doesn't think the U.S. would elect a woman as president, citing Harris and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's losses to Trump. She has said the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee should be a man if the party wants to win.
Hostin questioned whether president would be the right position for Harris during an April episode of "The View" and said she wished Harris had pursued a run for California governor.

"This goes right to the heart of what the Media Research Center has been arguing to the FCC about for months now. The View knowingly operates as a propaganda arm for the Democratic Party and for Democratic candidates," NewsBusters associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Sunny openly admitted that her intention with the question was to help Kamala with what she felt was a layup question that would lead to a slam-dunk answer. This incident was an abuse of ABC's privileged access to the public broadcast spectrum."

President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Bahrain during his tour of the Gulf region, as France continues to reel from a wave of violent protests.

The French leader is hoping to strengthen defence ties and secure oil and gas supplies amid major disruption to global fuel shipments arising from the US-Israel war on Iran. He has already visited Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as part of his three-day trip. His next stop is Qatar.
On the first day of Macron’s trip, France and Kuwait signed eight agreements and cooperation documents covering defence, artificial intelligence, investment and more.

Macron then met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi on Monday. The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to advancing cooperation in energy, advanced technology and artificial intelligence (AI).

According to the French Foreign Ministry, the UAE is France’s biggest importer in the Gulf, with bilateral trade standing at 10.8 billion euros ($12.1bn) in 2025. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) [PDF], France supplied 18 percent of the UAE’s arms and defence imports in 2025 – the second highest after the United States, at 42 percent.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London’s School of Security Studies, explained that Macron’s visit to the region is “symptomatic of a much larger geopolitical transformation”.

“We are witnessing the gradual emergence of a post-American Middle East in which Washington remains militarily powerful but increasingly struggles to exercise the political leadership it once enjoyed,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.

“Europe and the Gulf now face a remarkably similar strategic challenge. Both have become excessively dependent on American security decisions, and both are discovering that this dependence carries substantial economic and political costs.”
Most pressing for Macron is finding solutions for strife at home.

France has been engulfed in protests and violence over a proposed government budget seeking tens of millions of euros in savings to public spending. Protesters angry about the crumbling state of French schools and planned pay freezes for public-sector workers have taken to the streets in increasingly violent protests, and authorities have imposed curfews in some cities.

More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday as protesters demanded better education infrastructure and government steps to address the cost-of-living crisis. During weeks of protests, more than 2,500 people have been arrested, and demonstrations have descended into looting and arson in numerous locations.

A major issue is the spike in energy prices affecting all of Europe – much of it as a result of the Iran war – which has also fuelled growing public anger in France. Disruptions to the supply of refined oil products such as petrol and diesel caused by the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz have caused up to 20 percent of French petrol stations to run out of both at various times since the conflict began.
Macron’s visit to the Gulf, accompanied by senior executives from France’s two biggest energy groups, TotalEnergies and Engie, comes as oil prices hover above $100 a barrel.
What France needs most urgently, therefore, is new suppliers. Those look to have been secured.
On Tuesday, the UAE committed to supplying 100,000 tonnes (746,000 barrels) of diesel per month to France for an unspecified duration, according to Bloomberg.
Bahrain has agreed to supply 100,000 tonnes of diesel per month for an unspecified duration, while Saudi Arabia will provide 95,000 tonnes in each of October and November, via TotalEnergies.

Besides securing oil imports, however, France is also looking to boost its own exports, particularly of its defence equipment to the Gulf region, as the country suffers from record national debt – the highest level since the immediate aftermath of World War II, analysts say.
France has already strengthened its military partnership with Saudi Arabia, which has been battling the Iran-backed Houthi group from Yemen.

Last month, Macron said France would send troops and defence systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which is crucial for energy transport. Oil installations and airports in Saudi Arabia have come under attack from the Houthi group.

In late September, Macron said France would deploy what he termed “military means” to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Yanbu Red Sea oil terminal. Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, which carries oil from its eastern oilfields across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea, has come under attack during the Iran conflict. It is the country’s main means of continuing to export oil while the critical Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. But Yemen’s Houthis have also been attacking Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
Macron stated in a TV interview that “soldiers, radars, defence systems” would be sent.

While he did not give specifics about volumes, it was a move described by French newspaper Le Monde as marking “a geopolitical shift”, as defence cooperation between the two countries has previously been “discreet, ambiguous and marked by extreme caution when it came to defining it”, the newspaper noted.

Last week, France’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Pascal Confavreux, said again that “operational elements” to defend Saudi oil facilities had been put into action, without specifying which “military means” had been sent.

Meanwhile, on Monday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot met with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, to review bilateral relations and discuss regional developments. Barrot also reaffirmed France’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks.
Krieg assesses that France can offer Gulf states generally something that has become “increasingly valuable”: military capabilities not entirely dependent on the US.

“France can offer defence industrial cooperation, technology transfers, joint production, training and greater operational autonomy,” he said. “For countries such as the UAE and Qatar, this means progressively reducing their dependence on American weapons systems, spare parts, intelligence and political permissions.”
However, Krieg cautioned that the “central dilemma” for France is likely to be whether increasing its involvement in the region could draw it into the ongoing conflict.

“Consider the protection of Saudi energy infrastructure against Houthi attacks,” he said. “French air defence systems intercepting missiles would directly undermine the Houthis’ military strategy. If French forces are subsequently targeted, Paris could face pressure to retaliate. What begins as a defensive deployment could gradually become an operational commitment with much wider implications.”
Krieg explained that the same is likely to apply to naval deployments around the Strait of Hormuz, adding that “escalation in one theatre can rapidly affect another”.
France’s ties with Iran have already been strained over tit-for-tat diplomatic expulsions and political rhetoric against each other.
In July and August, France strongly condemned Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

In July, two French Embassy staff members were detained in Tehran and then declared personae non gratae. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said the diplomats had “interfered in Iran’s internal affairs under the pretext of engaging with civil society”.
In August, French Foreign Minister Barrot expelled two Iranian diplomats in retaliation.

Speaking at the Global Security Forum in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Tuesday, US Envoy Tom Barrack said that Washington is moving away from its traditional security-for-oil relationship with the Middle East and no longer seeks to dominate the region.
“The US no longer wants to own,” said Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy for Syria. “The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We’re not leaving.”

The pact, signed on August 7, contains 16 articles, according to the document submitted to the Turkish parliament, seen by the Reuters news agency.
It aims to create a joint defence architecture in the region, in the case of an armed attack on any member, and lays out provisions in each article accordingly.
In Article 1 of the accord, for example, the signatories shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity.
Once the first article is invoked, in case of an attack on any member state, the document lays out provisions for what follows next, as outlined in Article 2 of the draft seen by Reuters.

“In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them,” says Article 2.
This point is similar to Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, NATO’s founding document, which treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all.

Article 2 goes on to say that each signatory – Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye – “will decide on the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required”, adding that the three countries will cooperate within their available resources, including military capabilities and resources.

Earlier this month, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

Articles 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the draft agreement, submitted to the Turkish parliament, also lay out details on defence industry cooperation, intelligence sharing, logistical support and joint training and the fight against “all means of terrorism”, including at the operational level.
Other provisions talk about joint research, development and innovation projects in the field of advanced technology and ensuring military readiness.
There is also mention of setting up a defence committee, which will include foreign and defence ministers from all three signatory states.
And there is a mechanism for allowing other states to join the agreement, with aspirants needing the approval of all three founding members.
The agreement will last 10 years, after which any country can withdraw according to the draft submitted to the Turkish parliament.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar speaking on the submitted pact said the process of ratification is going to take “quite some time”, despite the ruling coalition needing a simple majority.

“The various political parties that are represented in the Turkish parliament are going to discuss the provisions in the pact, and we could witness heated debates because the opposition has its own objectives,” he said.
Serdar said even if the deal is ratified, it would not lead to a deployment of Turkish troops, a move which will require other legislative processes.

Turkiye’s parliamentary speaker will refer the agreement to the parliament’s foreign affairs commission. The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, according to a source who spoke to Reuters.
Once it is submitted to the commission, the contents and details of the agreement are expected to be made public.

“This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to strengthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region,” Burhanettin Duran, the Turkish presidency’s communications director, said on X.
Duran added that the process marked an important milestone towards the “institutionalisation” of strategic cooperation between the three nations.
On Monday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan spoke of the escalating violence between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.
“As I often say, we are surrounded by a ring of fire. That is exactly the situation we face,” Erdogan said, while referring to the Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone attacks against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured commitments for an extra 200,000 tonnes of diesel a month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, according to the French presidency.
The Elysee Palace announced the deals on Tuesday, before the president landed in Qatar.
His three-day Gulf tour, which also stops in Kuwait, follows a weekend of violent protests in France over the soaring cost of living, as the US-Iran war keeps energy prices high.
The presidency said the UAE had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month, while a further 100,000 tonnes monthly would be secured during Macron’s visit to Bahrain.
Together with deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just over 10 percent of its consumption, it said.

Kuwait has also given “very clear commitments” to deliver diesel and kerosene to the French overseas territories of Mayotte and Reunion in the Indian Ocean, the presidency said. The shipments will go via Oman to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Patrick Pouyanne, the head of French oil giant TotalEnergies, who is travelling with Macron, said the deals would “reassure the French”.
“We are not going to run out of diesel in February,” he said, according to the AFP news agency.
Andreas Krieg, a professor at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that France’s energy deals fit a wider pattern.
He noted that Gulf states have sent delegations to London, Paris, Berlin and Rome in recent months, seeking access to military complexes and possible stakes in European defence companies.
“They see a growing entanglement between their interests and European interests,” he said. “Not just in the energy field,” but also supply chains, he added.
Both sides feel pressure from a United States that is increasingly sidelining them, creating an opening to minimise dependence on Washington, Krieg said.

Macron’s agenda in Qatar includes discussions about security, defence, securing energy commitments to France, and advancing the frontiers in artificial intelligence, according to Sheikha Alanoud Hamad Saud Al Thani, a political analyst and fellow at the Middle East Council for Global Affairs.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, she said Qatar “really valued” its ties with France, which is one of the Gulf state’s oldest defence relationships.
“It comes as no surprise that the French are one of Qatar’s most important friends in Europe,” she said, describing Macron’s visit as “extremely consequential”.
“[Qatar is] leveraging existing relationships to adapt to this new kind of asymmetrical warfare, and we’re looking to see advancements in anti-drone and defence capabilities,” she said.
Iran has blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the main exit route for the Gulf’s energy exports, sending crude prices soaring during the eight-month conflict. Diesel has been among the hardest hit.
The G7, chaired this year by France, agreed earlier in October to draw up to 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves.
France has also released 10 million barrels of diesel from its own reserves, aiming to cut prices by 12 to 18 cents a litre, or about 5 to 8 percent, from next month, the French presidency said.
As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report.

The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain.

While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine, China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems.
Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones, which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran.
Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated.

"The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW.
Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions

The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017, which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years.

"The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit."

"This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine," Song added.
"Life in North Korea is not easy, but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said.
The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity."

"These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done."

Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic."

Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights" and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations.
The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said.

"UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added.
North Korea developing its drone capabilities

It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances.

"And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North.

To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible.

It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected.

The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.
There are only a few days left until Brazil's runoff election on October 25, with neither left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva nor right-wing populist Flavio Bolsonaro a clear favorite.
While three polls from last week showed a razor-thin lead for Bolsonaro, the PoderData polling institute has now projected 50% voter backing for each candidate.

This election could end up as close as the one held in 2022, when Lula narrowly beat Flavio Bolsonaro's father, Jair Messias Bolsonaro, with just 50.9% of the vote. Jair Bolsonaro, incidentally, was later jailed for attempting a coup to hold onto power.

His son, Flavio, surprisingly won the first round of voting on October 4 by securing 47% of the vote. Bolsonaro's right-wing bloc also won many additional seats in Congress, primarily at the expense of Brazil's centrist parties. And in the week following the first round of voting, polls showed Bolsonaro commanding a lead of up to six percentage points.

Yet last week, Lula managed to gain momentum through nationwide mass rallies and his dynamic social media presence. Bolsonaro, in contrast, had scaled back street campaigning in light of his strong poll numbers.
That turned out to be a mistake. Now he, too, is once more mobilizing supporters to stage major rallies across Brazil as the country readies for the runoff.
The rivalry between Lula's left-wing camp and Bolsonaro's far-right bloc has shaped Brazilian politics for the past decade.

Jair Bolsonaro gained nationwide recognition during the 2016 impeachment proceedings against Lula's political protegee, then-President Dilma Rousseff. He went on to win the 2018 presidential election while Lula was serving a prison sentence on corruption charges.
But when Lula's conviction was overturned, the former trade union leader staged a political comeback in 2022.
This polarization is responsible for the disappearance of centrist parties and a political alternative, or "third way," said political scientist Marco Aurelio Nogueira.

"The divide between Lula and Bolsonarism has paralyzed Brazilian politics, and anything that didn't belong to one pole or the other has disappeared," Nogueira told DW. This polarization is fueled by social media, the expert added, saying that "platforms' algorithms thrive on conflict and reward excitement."
Flavio Bolsonaro a toned-down version of his father
Nogueira said Flavio Bolsonaro's calm demeanor could explain why he has a realistic chance of defeating Lula, unlike his father in 2022.

"Jair Messias Bolsonaro was a crude, rhetorically aggressive figure," said Nogueira. "Flavio Bolsonaro, on the other hand, casts himself as more moderate and gives Bolsonarism a more youthful image. He communicates skillfully, posts well-produced videos, and addresses workers' issues, such as the introduction of the five-day workweek."

Lula's recent promise to shorten workweek hours has lent momentum to his campaign. Alarmed by Lula's rising poll numbers, Bolsonaro gave up his opposition to the move and voted in favor of the five-day workweek.

Bolsonaro is now taking a less radical stance on fiscal policy, too. Although he had announced drastic budget cuts before the first round of voting, modeled on the policies of his libertarian Argentine ally Javier Milei, he now intends to continue Lula's social programs. That said, Bolsonaro has not presented a plan for how he intends to reduce Brazil's high public debt.
Banco Master corruption scandal shapes race

The election campaign has been overshadowed by a massive corruption scandal surrounding the insolvent financial institution Banco Master. Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's former owner, is under investigation for fraud, money laundering and corruption.

Vorcaro is accused of having bribed decision-makers in the world of politics, finance and the judiciary. Several Supreme Court justices are said to be involved in the scandal, which involved dubious sex parties and millions in reported payouts. Judges from both the Lula camp and some appointed by Jair Bolsonaro are said to be tied up in the scandal.

Flavio Bolsonaro is alleged to have accepted goods and services from Vorcaro, including a €10 million donation for a film about his father's life. Yet Lula has not been able to capitalize on his rival's alleged failings. After all, his very own son is implicated in another corruption scandal. Moreover, Bolsonaro has repeatedly drawn attention to Lula's 2017 conviction for corruption, even though it was later overturned by the Supreme Court.
Political scientist Nogueira believes the mudslinging between both candidates over who is more corrupt has left voters jaded.

"There are constant reports about scandals and mutual accusations from all sides," said Nogueira. "As a result, the effect is essentially canceled out in the election campaign. The average voter tunes out and no longer attaches much importance to these accusations when making a voting decision."

Both candidates held their first live television debate on Sunday. On Friday, two days before the runoff election, they will face off once more on Brazil's largest broadcaster, Globo. The debate will likely have a significant influence on the October 25 vote.
Experts believe the key for both candidates will be to not be rattled by provocations from the other side. Concrete policies, in turn, will only play a minor role in the debate.

On July 20, Navkiran Natt and her partner set out for the magistrate's office in New Delhi to get married. They arrived to find a tense situation, with police gathering to break up a youth-led march on Parliament. Office staff — and couple's wedding witnesses — running late due to barricades.
The protest movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had announced the march to demand the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The protesters were met with heavy resistance from security forces, who had deployed batons, tear gas shells and pellet-firing shotguns, leading to injuries and mass detentions.
Less than three months later, on October 10, Natt left home early in the morning and spent the day crisscrossing the locked-down Indian capital looking for a protest she could join.

"The success of this protest is not how many people will reach Jantar Mantar," she told DW, referring to the protest site in central New Delhi. "It's that even after all this barricading and state violence, people are leaving their homes to join."

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

After succeeding in seeing Pradhan step down in late July, the CJP is now demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.
With CJP leadership in judicial custody or under threat of detention, one name has fast become synonymous with the demonstrations: student leader Neha Bora, who prefers to use the pronoun they/them.

Bora has run through the streets to dodge police officials, climbed barricades in the face of security personnel, shouted slogans from detention vans, and addressed press conferences alongside CJP spokespersons and others.
They are the president of the All India Students' Association (AISA), the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation (CPI-ML).
"In extremely disappointing, fearful, tyrannical times, people try to gather hope from whatever source they can … If these people are fighting, then probably we can also fight," Bora told DW.
"It is a responsibility that you owe to people," they added.
Women out on the streets in large numbers

The Cockroach-led demonstrations also come at a time when women and members of the LGBTQ+ community are calling for greater autonomy for women in the aftermath of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi late last month, placing the issue of safety in India back into the spotlight.

According to the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), 441,534 cases of crimes against women were registered in 2024, averaging 1,210 cases per day. Experts say these official statistics can only give a partial account of gendered violence.
But despite facing sexualized backlash from police on the streets and from online mobs, the women and genderqueer people leading the movement reject being cast as victims.
"The "beti bachao" [save the daughter] thing just doesn't cut it with this generation. It is a very specific ask: see us as political beings, free beings," activist Kavita Krishnan told DW.
"Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao" (Save the Daughter, Educate the Daughter) is a flagship BJP government program launched in 2015.
These days, Gurmeher Kaur's day starts like any other — a workout or a yoga class — and often ends with Indian Youth Congress's lawyers getting her released from police detention.
"Resistance can't be a separate event … a big day, and then you go back to your regular life," she told DW.
The 29-year-old author of "The Young and the Restless: Youth and Politics in India" spent a better part of the last decade in the public eye.
This year, she joined the youth wing of India's main opposition party, The Congress, whose offices are located a stone's throw away from Jantar Mantar, the hub of the last wave of protests.
She said her political association has given her access to resources that can support the movement, offering a safety net for protesters "regardless of their political affiliation."
At a time when authorities are cracking down on CJP protesters, she said opposition members like her have a duty to fulfill: "Show up, put your body on the line."
But showing up often comes with a cost, especially for women and queer protesters.
Kaur explains how male colleagues often "feel quite elated when their photos are in the media." However, for her, "attention is equal to death and rape threats and humiliation and abuse."
Natt, an activist most significantly associated with the 2020–2021 farmers' protests, echoes Kaur's experience.
"If a woman is leading the protest, the first attack is on her sexuality," she said.
Social media images have shown women protesters with their clothes torn during clashes with police.
Delhi officials have denied allegations of manhandling, adding that women protesters were treated with "dignity."
Bora refutes the police's claim, saying that a small number of female personnel were available to handle a large number of women protesters.
"Several women protesters came to protect me and prevent me from getting detained," they said.

Authorities have registered a police case against a journalist who accused a senior Delhi police officer of sexual harassment under an Indian law meant to prevent crimes against members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs). They say her own allegations are under investigation.
The internet was also flooded with AI-made, sexualized images of women protesters edited into protest photos.
This has not prevented protesters from taking to the streets even the day after being detained by authorities.
"They don't know what they're dealing with," Krishnan said, referring to the government's crackdown on demonstrators.
She said authorities assume sexual humiliation will scare women off, but "this is not a generation that thinks of… sexual violence as being something shameful."

She was at the forefront of demonstrations after the 2012 "Nirbhaya" gang rape, where slogans like "Hang the rapists" were seen in public. This time, however, she said the anger "is not going to be about masculine displays of honor."
It is about "dignity and freedom ... Women face all kinds of problems in every country, and Indian women are no different," she added.

She said the youth-led protests are part of a wider global wave of "civilizational, cultural nationalism," which uses gender and the language of protection, whether of daughters, families or tradition, to rally support against minorities, immigrants and trans people.

"You listen to the rhetoric of Donald Trump or Viktor Orban or the Alternative for Germany (AfD). It is the same," she said, referring to politics in the United States and Europe. "If you look at what's happening in India, you may be able to better understand what's happening in your country."
These young Indians, she said, are refusing to be taken in. They are "fighting back for a language of the future, a language that has hope."
The 4 main alternate theories not presented at O.J. Simpson's murder trial and why they're all problematic
New York Times reports that a late, convicted drug trafficker once gave information about murder weapon

The possibility that O.J. Simpson had a previously unknown accomplice dispose of a knife after he'd committed a double homicide has been raised after a just-published New York Times investigation, based on unsealed court files and recently conducted interviews.
Simpson's murder acquittal in connection with the brutal slayings of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her acquaintance Ron Goldman has been widely debated since 1995.

In the prosecution's view, Simpson — who had physically abused his former wife — lay in wait outside her Los Angeles house in the hours between attending a recital by his youngest daughter and leaving for the airport to fly to Chicago. He was triggered by rejections of different sorts from both Brown Simpson and his girlfriend that day, they alleged.

Simpson's defence team asserted that the pro football Hall of Famer was at his residence all night, and that the Los Angeles Police Department investigation was both error-ridden and nefarious, with allegations that evidence was planted both at his property and the crime scene.

Both sides suggested that Goldman — who was returning glasses to Brown Simpson's residence left at the restaurant where he worked — was an unintended victim. No knives have ever been located and connected to the murders.
A YouGov poll taken after Simpson's April 2024 death found that, of those who had an opinion, 61 per cent thought Simpson did commit the murders, while 11 per cent said he did not.
Here are the most-discussed alternate theories outside of the view that Simpson acted alone in committing the murders and disposing of any weapons or clothing on June 12, 1994.

Simpson — years before participating in a book that included a hypothetical of how he might have committed the crimes — wrote in a 1994 book that "the answer to the deaths of Nicole and Mr. Goldman lies somewhere in the world that Faye Resnick inhabited."

Resnick was a confidante of Brown Simpson who spent considerable time at her residence. Just days before her murder, Brown Simpson organized an intervention for Resnick who was struggling with cocaine use.

Cochran heads into to a New York courtroom, on March 16, 2001. He led Simpson's high-powered criminal defence team, and suggested Colombian drug dealers might have been to blame for the killings. (Stephen Chernin/The Associated Press)

Simpson defence attorney Johnnie Cochran asked a police detective at trial about "Colombian neckties," seemingly equating Brown Simpson's injuries to a supposed method of killing sometimes employed by Colombian drug dealers.
Cochrane was denied by the judge a full airing of a theory that he spoke to reporters about — that Brown Simpson was killed by dealers in a case of mistaken identity related to Resnick's coke debts.
A Colombian anti-drug police chief told The Associated Press in 1995 the "neckties" were not a method he'd seen used in the country's many drug-related killings of that era.

The Jason Simpson theory involves a person that the LAPD actually considered, at least according to homicide investigator Tom Lange. Like a few others in his father's orbit, Jason — born to Marguerite Whitley, Simpson's first wife — lawyered up and could not be interviewed.

Longtime private investigator William Dear, since deceased, was the foremost proponent of this theory, in the 2000 book O.J. Is Guilty But Not of Murder. Dear leans heavily on the fact that the the younger Simpson had access to many knives while working in the restaurant industry and had experienced some brushes with the law.
Jason Simpson, left, sits with his cousin Terri Baker, centre, and his sister Arnelle, in a Los Angeles courtroom on Jan. 23, 1995. (Rick Meyer/AFP/Getty Images)

Dear asserts that Jason killed two people by himself less than 30 minutes after finishing a restaurant shift and dropping off his girlfriend. He then supposedly called his father to help out at the crime scene. The motive? Jason was under the impression that his former stepmother had agreed that his restaurant would host the post-recital dinner of family members, but they went to Goldman's place of employment instead.

If the theory is correct, we are to believe that the father left his own blood at the crime scene — having arrived after the homicides occurred — but the perpetrator, his son, did not while killing two people in violent and sustained attacks.

In My Brother the Serial Killer, aired in 2012 by Investigation Discovery, various members of convicted killer Glen Rogers's family claim he bragged about committing the Brown Simpson and Goldman murders. But the stories they relayed were sometimes convoluted and even contradictory — one involved Rogers hired to do work at Brown Simpson's house and another suggested he was hired only to commit a robbery and the deaths weren't part of the plan.
Convicted killer Glen Rogers, right, appears in a Tampa, Fla., court on July 8, 1996. He was executed in Florida last year. (Chris O'Meara/The Associated Press)
The Brown Simpson and Goldman killings doesn't fit the pattern of Rogers's known and suspected murders, which involved women seen at bars with Rogers and left dead just hours later.

A former prosecutor said at the time of the show's airing that Rogers was cynically trying to prevent his own death penalty sentence, while Goldman's sister, Kim, blasted the cable network's decision to air the program as irresponsible. The LAPD said there was no reason to believe Rogers was involved.
Rogers was executed by the state of Florida in May 2025.

Twice-convicted drug trafficker Joey Ippolito, the Times has recently learned, was a friend to Al Cowlings, the former football player who famously transported Simpson in a white Ford Bronco on a hours-long drive after the warrant for his arrest was announced.

Ippolito, in a 1990s federal drug case in New York, reportedly offered information on where and how the murder weapon was disposed. But, per the newspaper, the court document containing that broad description does not "specify what he said, or to what degree he implicated himself or others."
If the theory is to believed, Ippolito — who died in 2006 — participated as an accomplice to murder just a few months after escaping a Florida prison.

Al Cowlings, a longtime friend of O.J. Simpson, is shown at a news conference in Los Angeles on Feb. 15, 1995. The New York Times has reported that a criminal friend of Cowlings once told investigators in an unrelated case that he had knowledge concerning the murder weapon used in the killings of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. (Reuters)

Sam Ippolito recounted in great detail his brother's participation to the Times, but then recanted after being denied payment for his story. According to the Times, many friends and family branded Sam as an unreliable narrator while also rejecting the possibility Joey was involved in any way in the Los Angeles murders.

The Times strangely describes the double homicide as "efficient" even though a glove and a hat were found at the scene, in addition to a voluminous amount of blood and several footprints. Any theory placing a second person at the murder scene would have to contend with how two people left behind those items.

In addition, the blood evidence at the scene and inside Simpson's Bronco was connected only to him and the two victims. Brown Simpson was nearly decapitated, and Goldman suffered about 30 knife wounds while fighting for his life.
As well, the footprints at the scene not belonging to Goldman — Brown Simpson was barefoot — were connected to one pair of shoes, the prosecution contended.

A compressed timeline poses challenges to all alternate theories of an accomplice. While the prosecution and defence sparred over the timeline, it is generally believed that about 90 to 100 minutes passed between when Simpson returned from a McDonald's with his house guest Kato Kaelin and when he entered a limo to take him to the airport. In between, he placed a cellphone call to his girlfriend, who had apparently left him a breakup voicemail.

About 20 minutes of that time would be needed for a drive back and forth between the crime scene and his residence. In addition, Simpson would have had to successfully make contact with an accomplice or accomplices.

The limo driver saw no other vehicles arriving to Simpson's home, though it is true that a few hours lapsed between when Simpson left for the airport and when homicide detectives descended upon his property.
Japan launches spacecraft to mysterious moons of Mars
1st mission to Mars's moons will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos
A Japanese spacecraft rocketed toward Mars on Tuesday on an unprecedented quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.
Five of the world's space agencies joined forces for the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars's two pint-sized moons.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country's main spaceport on Tanegashima Island. Officials declared success an hour later when the spacecraft separated as planned from the rocket's upper stage. Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet, shaking hands and embracing.

While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons.
If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031.
"There's a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow," said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who's involved with the project.
Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt.

Employees of Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency and others celebrate at the Tanegashima Space Centre as a Japanese spacecraft launched aboard an H3 rocket successfully separated as planned on Tuesday. (Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/The Associated Press)
Mars's moon Phobos is a lumpy, little rock
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 22 kilometres or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars's moons — and possibly moons elsewhere — came to be.

Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $812 million ($578 million US) mission features a hefty five-tonne spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos's tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that's named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.
This photo taken with NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, shows Phobos, one of Mars's moons, on March 23, 2008. No spacecraft has ever gone there before. (NASA/The Associated Press)
No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon's extraordinarily low gravity.
What happens after Idefix the rover lands

The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency's Julien Baroukh. Once the rover's solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial one millimetre per second (0.04 inches per second).

Idefix will serve as a "scout for safety," according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency unveils a spacecraft for its Martian Moons eXploration mission at the Tanegashima Space Center in Minamitane, Japan, on Aug. 13, 2026. (Yuika Kawazoe/Kyodo News/The Associated Press)

The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least 10 grams (one-third of an ounce) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighborhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert.
It's a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path.
The moons' names aren't exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They're the twin sons of the god of war Ares (Mars in Roman mythology).
Scientists hope to learn how Mars's moons formed

Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavours. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars?

By studying Mars's moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It's also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars's gravity.

Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life.
The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including those by astronauts, said NASA's acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays.
"It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system," said the Germany Space Agency's rover chief Markus Grebenstein.

Japan isn't the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system's rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving.
Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031.

Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $122 million ($87 million US), the French Space Agency about $95 million ($68 million US), the German Space Agency about $79 million ($56 million US) and the European Space Agency some $24 million ($17 million US).
Death toll in Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces rises to 73: governor
Strike on southern Yemen training camp is deadliest since fighting began escalating in July

The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 73 people, all new recruits, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country began escalating three months ago, a senior Yemeni government official said Tuesday.

The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, and some were still missing a day after the Iranian-aligned rebels hit the al-Alam training camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, provincial governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir told The Associated Press.

Monday's strike was part of a recent surge of fighting in Yemen, which started when forces from the internationally-recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped fighting in the country's civil war.
The Houthis have also fired missiles and drones on Saudi Arabia, which has struggled to counter the Houthi attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms.

The strike on the al-Alam camp hit while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. Videos from the area circulated online and analyzed by The Associated Press showed many motionless bodies lying on the sandy ground of the camp.
The strike also wounded more than 200 other recruits, the governor said.
The casualties were new recruits from across Shabwa being trained to provide security in the province and not for combat operations, he said.
"This had nothing to do with front lines," he said. "They had not attacked anyone or advanced against anything. It was only to protect the security of their province."

Another government official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief the media, said several suffered serious injuries and were transferred to hospitals in other provinces in life-threatening condition. He said at least 15 of the recruits killed were from a single Yemeni tribe.

The Shabwa provincial government said in a statement Monday that the Houthis fired three ballistic missiles on the camp. The Houthis claimed the attack, saying they had killed and wounded dozens but did not provide further details.
People wait at a gas station to fill up cooking gas cylinders in the southwestern city of Taiz, Yemen, on Monday. (Anees Mahyoub/Reuters)

The camp, which was previously used by a militia backed by the United Arab Emirates, is located in the Jardan district, north of the provincial capital of Ataq. It sits on a crucial supply line connecting to the government-controlled province of Marib.

Shabwa and Marib, along with neighbouring Hadramawt province, contain what has been dubbed the Yemeni government's "triangle of power," a strategic area in which the country's oil and gas production is located.

On Tuesday, authorities in Saudi Arabia issued an attack warning for the capital area in the late morning followed by the sound of an explosion in northern Riyadh where the King Khalid International Airport is located. The airport has come under repeated Houthi attacks this month, forcing the facility to suspend its operations.
The all-clear was given a short time later and Saudi Arabia said a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis had been intercepted.
Yemen first plunged into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile.

A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year in an attempt to restore the government to power. The conflict created one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters, and killed more than 150,000 people.

Meanwhile, the U.K. announced Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia against the Houthis to include "defensive" air patrols by Royal Air Force jets, but stressed there is no military solution to the conflict.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said British Typhoon jets will "conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia, helping to protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure" from missiles and drones fired by the Iran-backed rebels in Yemen.
He said the British planes won't strike Houthi targets.
- Yemen's Houthis attack presidential palace in Aden, key Saudi infrastructure
- Saudi-led coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
- Britain to give limited military support to Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi rebels
The U.K. will also send a military transport plane and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia, Streeting said.
The announcement follows Britain's decision last month to offer in-air refuelling of Saudi planes operating against the Houthis. That mission is being extended by another 90 days, Streeting said.

The defence secretary said in a written statement to Parliament that "the government remains clear that there is no long-term military solution to the conflict in Yemen," however. "We continue to support a UN-led political process as the best route to a durable peace," he said.
Federal MPs have told the ABC they are afraid for their safety after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
MPs said some of the security measures available to them were infrequent or "lacklustre", while others like threat assessments for their homes had not been offered.
The Australian Federal Police Association has called for privately contracted security assessments of MP homes to be brought under the AFP.

Federal MPs have described deep fears for their safety in the wake of the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, with some describing a mixed experience of the security services made available to them.

The Australian Federal Police Association says police protection for MPs and the threat assessments conducted for them must be reviewed, and have called for privately contracted home security inspections to be taken over by the AFP.

While ministers and high-profile individuals receive regular protection and threat assessments, other MPs described infrequent or "tokenistic" threat assessments — in some cases, MPs said they had never been offered risk assessments for their home security.

The attack on Ms Haines outside her Wangaratta electorate office in regional Victoria has shaken federal politicians, particularly because Ms Haines is considered well-liked and less at risk than higher profile or more controversial MPs.
Australian Federal Police Association president Alex Caruana said the number of MPs expressing safety fears was increasing.
"Certainly the experience I have had is MPs ringing me and saying they are feeling unsafe," Mr Caruana said.

"We need to make sure that not just that particular person is safe but their entire family. And the number of politicians and the number of MPs that have rung me to say, 'Hey, I feel safe but my family don't feel safe,' … has increased significantly."
National security agencies have repeatedly warned of the growing threat of politically motivated violence.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed more than 1,000 threats to federal politicians had been identified by security agencies in the most recent financial year, and every federal MP that the ABC spoke to described receiving death threats, with some also describing court action resulting from threats made to them, particularly online.

MPs, who spoke on background in order to protect their security arrangements, have described feeling exposed after an attack on a "delightful" regional MP with "non-aggressive politics", who would have been categorised as being at lower risk.
"I feel unsettled, that's how I feel. Unsettled and grieving," one MP said.
Another said, "As a woman in politics I feel pretty nervous at the moment."
"I am certainly not instilled with confidence they are doing all they can."
Minister for Women Katy Gallagher said colleagues had expressed fears for their safety to her.
"Yes, they are [afraid], and I don't think we should pretend otherwise," Senator Gallagher told ABC Afternoon Briefing yesterday.
AFP protection levels must be reassessed: police union

The AFP provides "close personal protection" to high-profile politicians, including MPs deemed to be at higher risk — though for many MPs that service is only periodic or in response to a specific threat.
Mr Caruana said two years ago there were far many more operational hours required than there were sworn officers to meet it, which had since been assessed and rebalanced.
But he said staffing levels would have to be revisited in the wake of the attack against Ms Haines.
"My gut feeling is we may have prioritised costs over safety in some of those instances," Mr Caruana said.

"I think it is very pertinent now that we look at what is the risk assessment, the real risk assessment, and what is the risk appetite of the people we are serving … What cost, what price do you put on that safety?"

The AFP received a little over half a billion dollars in the 2024-25 financial year to protect politicians and sensitive facilities, which the home affairs minister said received "a major increase" at the last budget.
At the 2025 federal election, more than 600 AFP personnel worked more than 45,000 operational hours to provide protective security to politicians and candidates campaigning across the country.
"Where we have landed now is nowhere near that. So we need to find that compromise, we need to find that balance," Mr Caruana said.

"I think it is important that we hear the politicians and their families and what they have to say, why they feel unsafe … sometimes something that can seem quite benign is actually something quite nefarious."
An AFP spokesperson said it did not comment on the specific protective security arrangements for MPs or its capabilities.
MPs have told the ABC the frequency of engagement with the AFP could vary, and that changes in roles or circumstances did not always prompt a fresh threat assessment.
One MP said they were caught off guard after changing roles and attending an event with their children, who were "terrified" when it was crashed by violent protesters.
A 24-hour contact point is available for MPs to report safety concerns, with a dedicated team resourced to investigate threats.

Senior home affairs, AFP and ASIO officers are preparing to update MPs tomorrow on the current threat environment, and will also encourage MPs to share their diaries in order to more proactively manage risks to their safety.

But MPs say for some safety tasks they have been left to themselves, and received "lacklustre" advice such as to vet constituents before meeting them, or not to share in advance that they will be attending an event.
"I am a politician, it is my job to reach out to the community and promote [that]," one MP said.
An AFP spokesperson said the agency had delivered six multi-agency briefings for MPs just this year, which included security awareness resources, engagement and reporting pathways.

One MP warned that a careful balance was needed, that engaging with the public was "fundamental to democracy, [and] you cannot lock your MPs away", and that 24/7 protection would not only be fiscally challenging but also a personal imposition most MPs did not want.
Community Strong MP Allegra Spender said she feared politicians pulling back from the very sort of "active, available and very locally engaged" politics that Ms Haines embodied.
"Security services will only get us so far, I think the bigger issue is culturally," Ms Spender said.
"I think a lot of us thought that something like this could easily happen, truthfully because of the level of aggression you see online, but also that you sometimes see on the streets."
Mixed experiences with home security for MPs

The AFP conducts individualised threat assessments for the highest-risk politicians, such as ministers on the National Security Committee of cabinet, or MPs with Jewish or Arabic backgrounds, but for those deemed lowest risk, threat assessments by the AFP are conducted at a group level.
Further assessments can be conducted in response to an incident or concern, either by the AFP or privately contracted firms.
For many MPs, residential assessments are also contracted to private security firms, which politicians have told the ABC has been a mixed experience.
At least two MPs said there had never been an offer made to them to assess their home security, and that changes in roles or taking on more senior positions did not prompt new threat assessments.
Another said they felt that residential assessment had been "tokenistic", and they had to self-fund some security measures.
Mr Caruana said those residential assessments should be brought under the AFP.

"In my opinion I think that is something that needs to be brought back in-house. Law enforcement agencies, whether it is ASIO, AFP or otherwise are the subject matter experts in this field, not discounting the private firms that are doing it, because I am sure they are doing a great job," Mr Caruana said.

"But we need to ensure we have got some consistency across the board … the AFP does their own risk assessments for residentials for some of our own high-profile members … so we have the capability already, we have the training."
New curfews have been implemented in Paris and in cities across France following destructive riots in the country.
Troops will also be deployed ahead of new protests planned against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
A major security operation, including the deployment of troops, will be in place ahead of planned protests this weekend.
Troops will be deployed and new curfews imposed in a bid to restore calm in France after a weekend marred by some of the most destructive protests in years.
On Tuesday, the French government acknowledged failures in its response to the weekend's riots that saw thousands arrested amid clashes with police, cars set alight and public buildings stormed.
The government said it would reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation ahead of more protests planned this weekend.
"The deployment next Saturday will be massive," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said.

But he said the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities as part of the nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
After a night of relative quiet, thanks in part to curfews, new public orders were implemented in Paris around the Place de la Republique from 11pm local time on Tuesday to 6am Wednesday.
On Monday night, police emptied and guarded the Place de la Republique with a helicopter overhead.

A ban has also been issued on any public gatherings from 8pm Tuesday in les Halles, near the presidential palace, the parliament and senate buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue, in the Vendome square where jewellery stores are located and near train stations.
In Lille, in the north, where the curfew only applied to minors, officers patrolled the city centre, checking bypassers' identities.
Marseille mayor Benoit Payan said there would also be curfews for minors around the commercial areas hardest-hit by the weekend's riots from Tuesday night.

Framing the crisis as a choice "between violence and the Republic", Mr Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating public anger over high living costs and declining public services.

Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence.

Meanwhile, police have arrested a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch-list and belonged to an ultra-left group.

The unrest shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.

Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes.
