Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East. The increase in crude prices threatened to drive up the cost of gas in the United States just two weeks before the midterm elections.

U.S. crude prices jumped as much as 5% to about $109 a barrel, the highest price since April, while the price of international Brent crude climbed 1.5% to more than $111, its highest price since May. Prices pulled back later in the morning, after weaker-than-expected U.S. housing starts raised the prospect of a broader slowdown and lower demand.
Prices for advanced oil contracts dated for next year also hit record highs, “implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Tuesday.

“The 2027 contracts are moving higher as well as the possible reality of higher for longer oil prices sink in,” Peter Boockvar, author of the Boock Report and chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said in a note Tuesday.
High gas prices have become a major issue for voters in the midterms, where Republicans face dwindling odds of maintaining their control of Congress.

A recent NBC News poll found that 67% of U.S. adults believe gas prices are a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. A majority also said that current economic conditions have caused them to change their spending habits.
U.S. gasoline prices had started off the week lower. At $4.28 a gallon, the national average price of unleaded was on pace to reach its lowest level in a month.
But that trend is likely to be upended as higher crude prices filter through to the pump.
Several factors were contributing to Tuesday’s oil price hikes.
The cost of chartering a large tanker vessel to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled since September, data shows.

Much of that increase is a risk premium, both for sailors and insurance. During the past two weeks, at least 18 vessels have been attacked in the strait, the ship-tracking group Kpler said in a note Monday.
The higher cost of transport has begun to offset the recent bump in supply from a growing number of ships moving through the strait.
The Iranian attacks on ships have also prompted investor speculation that the Trump administration will be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms, the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels also claimed Monday that they had hit airport, energy and military targets in Saudi Arabia, as well as a training camp in Yemen for that government’s security forces.
The U.K. will begin deploying fighter jets over Saudi Arabia to help protect against further Houthi attacks, the Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The entry of another country’s military into the regional hostilities was taken as a further sign of escalating tensions.

U.S. envoys were meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff had been set to meet with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said earlier. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was also joining the talks, it added.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.

“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.

Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”

Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.

Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.

Local media reported that one of Haines’ legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker in critical condition after car ramming

Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then did a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.

“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the network that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.
Political violence is extremely rare in Australia, where lawmakers are often out in public with little or no security and their accessibility is a point of national pride.

“It’s an Australian tradition to have a chat to a politician that you bump into at the shops,” Josh Roose, an associate professor of politics at Deakin University in Melbourne, told NBC News in an interview.
But threats are rising as political rhetoric becomes more extreme, officials and experts say, particularly since the Covid pandemic.

According to the Australian Federal Police, there were 1,067 incidents of threats, harassment, nuisance or offensive behavior against senior officeholders, parliamentarians and protected locations in the 2025-26 financial year, a 12% increase over the previous year and twice the number five years earlier.

In a 2023 study of Victoria state parliamentarians, 82% reported harassment and 85% reported threats of harm, said Josh Holloway, a senior lecturer in government at Flinders University in Adelaide, with female politicians more likely to face abuse.

Holloway said that Australian federal lawmakers, especially those in rural areas, typically work from “shopfront-style offices,” hold regular community meetings and attend local events without security.
Those practices may now come under scrutiny, “but reducing public access to their representatives can come with significant democratic cost,” he said in emailed comments.
Albanese said Tuesday that it was everyone’s responsibility to “turn the temperature down.”

“We can disagree with each other, but do it in a respectful way,” he told Australia’s “Today” show. “And that’s something that Helen Haines always was characterized by, was that respect that she showed to others right across the political spectrum.”

Albanese said later that he had spoken by phone with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who ran from his nearby shop to help detain Haines’ attacker in what Albanese said was “a great example of the Australian spirit.”
“I heard a loud bang, with no brakes. It was crazy,” Jefferies told reporters. “I just ran out the front to see what was happening.”
Jefferies, who said he removed a knife from the suspect’s pocket and pulled him out of the car, said a lot of people “just ran to help.”

Haines, a mother and grandmother who spent three decades working in rural health as a nurse and midwife and has a doctorate in childbirth, was first elected to Parliament in 2019, then re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Her family said in a statement that they were grateful for the “swift assistance of bystanders,” as well as first responders.
The increase in political threats in Australia follows a similar trend in the United States and other liberal democracies, Roose said.
“Australia always echoes what we’re seeing internationally, but sometimes slightly behind,” he said.
Since the pandemic, there has emerged a “level of extremist discourse that is unparalleled in Australian history,” Roose said, one that is highly influenced by politics in the U.S.
Australia, and particularly Victoria, had some of the strictest pandemic lockdowns in the world, which left residents feeling “imprisoned, but also disempowered,” he said.
Lingering feelings of resentment combined with the current high cost of housing, fuel and other necessities have contributed to a “deep hostility” toward the government, Roose said.

Politics in rural Australia, especially, have become “highly inflammatory,” he said, “because of the online space and the poverty and the desperation that, quite frankly, has seeped into these areas.”
Roose said the “paradox” was that the victim was Haines, who is not considered a polarizing figure and is “someone who’s grown up and spent most of their life in these regions.”
“It indicates, I suppose, the challenge facing democracies around the world,” he said.
Yemen war continues to force families from homes amid hunger and disease

More than 250,000 people have now fled renewed fighting in Yemen, the UN said on Tuesday, citing particular concern for those sheltering in the southwestern city of Taiz and the wider governorate, where access is “essentially blocked”.

“The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” said UN human rights chief Volker Türk.

In an appeal to Houthi fighters who he said had encircled Taiz City to allow aid in immediately, the High Commissioner for Human Rights noted that 32 civilians have been confirmed killed across the governorate, including 14 children and nine women. He warned of a significant uptick in the risk of death and injury as fighting moves closer to densely populated areas of the city.

The development follows the resumption last month of clashes between Houthi fighters – formally known as Ansar Allah – and the internationally recognized Government based in Aden, ending the relative calm brought about by the 2022 truce.
The situation in Taiz is particularly worrying because around half of those recently uprooted by the violence have sought shelter there.
“Taiz is certainly the number one concern at the moment in an ocean of concerns,” said Akhil Iyer, United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Representative in Yemen.

“Many people have fled repeatedly. They are arriving in already overcrowded camps or communities with little or no food. Clean water is almost non-existent when they arrive. They’ve literally arrived with just the clothes on their backs, and they have almost nothing left to sustain themselves.”
According to the UN World Food Programme (WFP), wheat flour stocks in affected areas of Taiz are nearly exhausted.

“This is an alarming development in a governorate that already faces some of Yemen’s highest levels of food insecurity,” with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels, Mr. Iyer stressed.

Briefing journalists from Aden, the UNICEF official described the deteriorating situation in conflict-affected areas, where “garbage is piling up – particularly in Taiz city – as sanitation services come to a halt”.
The ongoing hostilities have made it extremely difficult and dangerous for humanitarian agencies to reach vulnerable communities and deliver fuel and other necessities.
The result could be an even more acute health emergency in a country already facing outbreaks of cholera and measles, along with suspected cases of diphtheria and dengue.

“We are very worried about the water and sanitation situation in Taiz because diesel fuel is essential to run pumping stations in and around the city. Supplies have been threatened by the lack of access and the blockage of supply routes, particularly from Aden to Taiz city,” Mr. Iyer explained.

He noted that although UNICEF had pre-positioned enough ready-to-use therapeutic food before the conflict escalated early last month, the supplies could not be distributed to health facilities because “all of the routes are closed”.

“We’re calling on all parties to protect children and civilians, safeguard water systems and health facilities, and uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law. That includes allowing humanitarian actors access.”

World Health Organization (WHO) spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic reported that 12 hospitals in Taiz had approximately four days of fuel remaining. The oxygen cylinders they require are in “daily deficit”, while 115 of 127 essential medicines have sufficient stocks for about one week or less, he said.

Matthew Saltmarsh, spokesperson for the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), stressed that access problems were preventing aid teams from reaching those most in need, although protection activities continued “where access allows”.
“Let’s not forget that there are some 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers who are also urgently in need of support; most are from Somalia and Ethiopia,” he added.
‘Season of fear’: Escalating Israeli attacks on West Bank olive farmers, deadly strikes on Gaza

Israeli attacks on war-torn Gaza over the weekend killed at least six Palestinians, including children, despite a year-old ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settler violence continued through the ongoing olive harvest, with UN independent experts on Monday urging Israel to protect Palestinian farmers.
- West Bank: Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settlers over the past two weeks, with 200 olive harvest-related attacks documented since the start of September
- Gaza: Israeli attacks have continued to cause deaths and injuries as nearly one million Palestinians face winter flood risks
- Funding shortages have forced UN agencies to make major cuts to food programmes
Death, demolitions along so-called ‘yellow line’

In the Gaza Strip, deadly Israeli airstrikes, gunfire and shelling occurred alongside incursions, demolitions and reported shifts in the so-called “yellow line” imposed by Israel since the year-old ceasefire agreement.
The attacks raised concerns and risks of further displacement, according to the latest updates from the UN emergency aid coordination office, OCHA.

Local health authorities told OCHA 57 Palestinians were reported killed and 319 injured between 29 September and 12 October, bringing the total number of casualties since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement to 1,493 fatalities and 5,299 injuries.
Meanwhile, around 950,000 displaced people have been assessed as living in sites at medium to high risk of flooding, including over 400,000 at high risk.
Available supplies offered partial assistance to only 18 per cent of the 294,250 families requiring shelter support for the rainy season, OCHA reported.

Daily cooked-meal production has declined by 12 per cent to approximately 614,000 amid funding constraints, while shortages of fuel, engine oil and essential supplies threaten the continuity of health and water services, the UN agency said.
Settler violence must end: Independent experts
Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settler attacks in the occupied West Bank over the past two weeks, OCHA reported.
During the same period, 160 olive harvest-related settler attacks resulted in casualties, property damage or both while record demolitions displaced 96 Palestinians, the agency said.

UN independent human rights experts warned on Monday that Palestinian farmers are facing renewed threats as the annual olive harvest gets underway, urging Israel to guarantee their protection and safe access to their land.

“The olive harvest should be a time when farmers can enjoy, in safety and dignity, the food and livelihoods their nature and land provide, not another season of fear, loss, violence and destruction,” said the Human Rights Council-appointed experts, who are not UN staff and do not receive a salary.

“Israel is under an international legal obligation to end its occupation of Palestinian land, immediately cease new settlement activities, evacuate settlers from the Occupied Palestinian Territory and provide full reparation for the damage caused by its violations, including by returning land and allowing displaced Palestinians to return to their homes,” the experts said.

“The international community, especially States with power and influence, must exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians, halt and reverse the rapidly expanding policies and practices of annexation and ensure accountability for decades of violations of Palestinian rights under international law,” they said, warning that the situation could worsen following new Israeli orders for uprooting olive trees and restrictions on farmers in the West Bank.

Coast redwoods are iconic giants of the Pacific Coast, found only in a narrow band of land stretching from central California to southern Oregon. These towering trees—the tallest in the world—are adapted to the region’s relatively cool, moist climate, particularly the thick summer fog that blankets their canopies during the dry season. But in recent years, the area has been getting hotter, and the fog has been dwindling, raising questions about how these ancient trees will fare in a warming world.

Now, scientists say they have an answer. A study published September 22 in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences finds that coast redwoods slow photosynthesis when temperatures spike, a discovery that suggests climate change could be threatening the trees’ long-term health and survival.

Through photosynthesis, plants convert sunlight, water and carbon dioxide into oxygen and sugars, which provide the energy and building blocks they need to grow. As trees build trunks, branches, roots and leaves, they store some of that carbon in their tissues. Because of their large size, thick bark and long life spans, coast redwoods act as massive carbon sinks, keeping it out of the atmosphere for decades or even centuries.

To better understand how rising temperatures might be affecting these processes in coast redwoods, researchers studied trees growing in Garcia River Forest in Mendocino County, California, near the southern part of the species’ range. Once or twice a month from July 2022 through October 2024—a span that included two heat waves—they took measurements for individual leaves, colloquially called needles.

Their analyses revealed that, during bouts of extreme heat, the needles were up to 18 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than the surrounding air. “That’s a huge difference and indicates that the leaves are stressed to the point where they can’t thermoregulate effectively,” lead author Lily Klinek, an ecologist at the University of California, Davis, tells Live Science’s Sarah Wild.

Based on the temperature difference, the team suspects that the leaves’ stomata—small, pore-like openings that help release heat via water vapor—were at least partially closed to help the tree retain moisture. But stomata also play an important role in photosynthesis, taking in the carbon dioxide needed for the process, so the results also suggest that the higher temperatures could be hampering photosynthesis.
Did you know? The world’s tallest living tree

The world’s tallest living tree is a roughly 380-foot-tall coast redwood named Hyperion, located in California’s Redwood National Park. Discovered in 2006, Hyperion has been officially off-limits to visitors since 2022 because tourists kept veering off established trails and damaging the delicate forest ecosystem. The towering plant is estimated to be about 600 years old.

To measure the impact of heat on photosynthesis more directly, Klinek and colleagues collected samples from the lower canopies of younger coast redwoods, whose branches are easier to reach than those of massive old-growth trees. Back in the laboratory, the team submerged the leaves in water and exposed them to a range of temperatures between 72 degrees and 110 degrees. Though their stomata were open and they had access to all the necessary ingredients for photosynthesis, their photosynthesis rates declined as temperatures increased.

This suggests that high temperatures might be directly affecting the trees’ ability to photosynthesize, rather than indirectly by prompting them to close their stomata and reduce their carbon dioxide uptake.

The findings indicate that coast redwoods are “really temperature sensitive,” Christopher Still, an ecophysiologist at Oregon State University who was not involved with the study, tells Science News’ Allie Skalnik. “You don’t see this as much with other species necessarily.”

Taken together, the study suggests that rising temperatures spurred by climate change could diminish coast redwoods’ ability to photosynthesize and store carbon. But it remains unclear whether the effects are temporary, or whether heat waves cause lasting damage. The researchers also say they haven’t discovered the point of no return—how hot it would have to get, and for how long, for that damage to become irreversible.

“Right now, the temperatures are coming back to normal in the fall and winter and letting the trees recover,” Klinek tells Vox’s Neel Dhanesha. “But in five or ten years, if temperatures are even hotter and heat waves are even more frequent, we don’t really know if there would be a recovery.”

It takes more than a few tricks and a penchant for fetch to receive a prestigious animal award. A black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands just snagged one for her ability to sniff out “sea vomit,” a colloquial name for the carpet sea squirt, an invasive marine creature threatening the waters along Britain and Ireland, among other places.

On October 15, Sgiath (pronounced Skee-ah) was crowned Animal of the Year by the nonprofit International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW). The 6-year-old pooch and her handler, Texa Sim, a marine ecologist based near Glencoe, Scotland, were recognized for their pioneering work in marine conservation. According to IFAW, Sgiath is believed to be the first dog trained to sniff out carpet sea squirt—which, if left unchecked, can smother native species and colonize infrastructure like oyster farms and fisheries.

“Every year, the Animal of the Year award celebrates animals doing extraordinary things, but Sgiath’s story is like nothing we’ve seen before,” says Sharon Livermore, director of marine conservation at IFAW, in a statement sent to media. “Her trailblazing work demonstrates the remarkable potential of dogs to contribute to conservation science in entirely new ways.”

Originally trained as a mountain rescue dog, Sgiath was later taught to recognize the scent of the invasive marine species. She has successfully sniffed out hundreds of colonies of the sea squirt, Kate Stephens and Victoria Gill report for BBC News. In fact, Sim tells the outlet that when Sgiath catches wind of a sea squirt colony, she’s never wrong—even when she’s sniffing through layers of seaweed on tricky structures, like pontoons and oyster cages.

“She’s a natural,” Sim says. Since first training Sgiath in marine detection, Sim has added to the sea squirt-sniffing team: a 3-year-old Labrador named Uisge, described as a “protégé” in the statement.

The carpet sea squirt first appeared in the United Kingdom in 2008. Scientists suspect the organism hopped aboard ships from its native Japan. The creature, formally called Didemnum vexillum, has already spread up the British coast, and conservationists are worried it will expand further. The sea squirt thrives in warmer waters, leading to increased concern as climate change continues to induce higher sea temperatures.

These and other invasive organisms can drain ecosystems of valuable nutrients, depriving endemic wildlife, Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist at Bangor University in Wales, tells BBC News. “These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellers,” he says. In Europe, spotting and controlling these invasive populations costs millions of dollars each year.

But not touching them can prove disastrous: In 1969, an unchecked carpet sea squirt population nearly decimated a population of Portuguese oysters living off the coasts of Portugal and France, per Metro’s Sarah Hooper.

Carpet sea squirt colonies are hard to spot. They can be creamy white, tan, or even pale pink or orange, and they often cling to algae or seaweed, appearing like a layer of slime—or vomit. Traditional means of identification involve laboratory analysis and DNA testing, requiring valuable time and resources, Holly Evans reports for the Independent. Sgiath, on the other hand, needs just a nose.

Using dogs to sniff out invasive species is not a new practice. Conservationists have been putting pups to work on land for more than a century, Katherine Manwell reported for Midstory in 2024. The practice became more widespread only in recent decades.

“In the mid-’90s ... within the wildlife research community, there was a call for more noninvasive techniques for getting the same information that we [were] getting by trapping and radio-collaring all kinds of species and animals,” Alice Whitelaw, co-founder and director of programs at the U.S.-based nonprofit Working Dogs for Conservation, told the outlet.

While canines are not a catch-all, they tend to be more efficient and less invasive than other methods, per Midstory, allowing conservationists to identify and remove unwanted species without disrupting the environment.
However, Sgiath is unique: She’s not sniffing invasive critters on land; she’s hunting them at sea. The Labrador walks the beach, entering the water at low tide to sniff out any potential colonies.
“She just does a survey with her nose, essentially,” Sim tells BBC News. “She can pinpoint exactly where it is.”

Still, Sgiath and future sea squirt-sniffers in her mold cannot eradicate these colonies on their own. But “if we can identify the species earlier and more efficiently, it gives conservationists and site managers a much better chance of responding before the problem gets out of hand,” Sim says in the statement.
Archaeologists have discovered the remains of a Norse church in southern Greenland, a find that could offer new insights into the lives of the Vikings who once called the island home.

“Churches were vital in Norse society, which makes them key to understanding how their society, especially the power structures, developed,” Christian Edelfelt Koch Madsen, an archaeologist with the National Museum of Denmark and co-leader of the dig, says in a statement.

Norse settlers from Iceland, also referred to as Vikings, first settled in Greenland around 985 C.E., led by explorer Erik the Red. They lived on the massive island until the early 15th century, when they mysteriously vanished.

As Tim Folger wrote for Smithsonian magazine in 2017, Norse settlers didn’t “just get by” in Greenland. They “built manor houses and hundreds of farms; they imported stained glass; they raised sheep, goats and cattle; they traded furs, walrus-tusk ivory, live polar bears and other exotic arctic goods with Europe.” Such success, he adds, makes their disappearance all the more perplexing.

For decades, researchers have been conducting archaeological excavations in hopes of better understanding the rise and fall of Norse society in Greenland. In the early 2000s, researchers discovered a rectangular stone wall with the remains of a stone building in the middle, a layout that suggests the site was once home to Norse church. But to definitively confirm the building’s purpose, they wanted to find a cemetery.

In 2025, archaeologists once again revisited the site. On the final day of that excavation, researchers started unearthing bits of charcoal, which suggested humans had once occupied the site. Then, they found what appeared to be a decomposed human bone.

When researchers returned this past August, they uncovered the remains of an entire human skeleton buried with its arms placed by its sides and its head pointing east, a positioning that suggests a Norse Christian burial sometime during the early Middle Ages.

“This is ‘the smoking gun.’ Now there is no doubt that this is a church,” Madsen says in the statement. That would make it the first Norse church discovered in Greenland in more than 60 years. Based on its size and construction from hewn stones, the researchers suspect it dates between 1100 and 1300 C.E., a period that aligns with when Norse settlers in Greenland were transitioning to Christianity.

The church is located near the modern town of Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, roughly three miles from Brattahlíð, the estate of Erik the Red and the primary hub for the entire Norse colony in Greenland, which numbered 3,000 individuals at its peak, Madsen tells the Viking Herald’s Jonathan Bennett.

In total, researchers have discovered the remains of six churches around Brattahlíð, likely constructed by rich local farmers or landlords. The researchers suspect they were competing for the religious power—and revenue—that accompanied church ownership. “These churches seem to demonstrate that, in the early Middle Ages, [Norse settlers] started competing about who’s going to run the show,” Madsen tells the Viking Herald.
- Born in Norway, Erik the Red left for Iceland after his father was exiled for manslaughter.
- During Erik’s own subsequent banishment from Iceland, the explorer first reached Greenland with a small group of men around 982 C.E. and returned three years later to start a settlement.
The site appears to correspond with a “Church Under the Sunny Mountains” mentioned in a medieval Icelandic manuscript called the Flateyjarbók, or the “Book of Flatey.”

The remains sit in front of a mountain range on the edge of the Greenland ice sheet, an area that often has sunny weather. However, as Madsen tells the Viking Herald, “there are a lot of mountains and a lot of places that look the same in Greenland.” The document mentions two other churches that could be nearby.

Looking ahead, the team plans to study the artifacts discovered during the recent dig. If they’re able to secure more funding, they hope to return to the church and narrow down when it was constructed.

In the meantime, they are still reveling in the success of the recent excavation, which “is another piece of the puzzle that may bring us closer to understanding what happened to the Norse colony in Greenland and the mystery of why it disappeared,” Konrad Smiarowski, an environmental archaeologist at the University Museum of Bergen and co-leader of the project, says in a statement, per High North News’ Trine Jonassen.

CRASH Network’s Insurer Report Card survey opens Nov. 1, and John Yoswick filled Repairer Driven News in on how the three-minute survey garners important information for the collision repair industry and consumers.

“The key reason that we believe shops should participate is the Insurer Report Card can then help educate consumers,” said Yoswick, CRASH Network’s editor. “We get 1,000 shops participating, and the result is a free report that anyone can download, including consumers, showing grades for 90-plus insurers.”
It asks collision repairers to grade each company from A+ to F based on how well the insurers’ claims practices help ensure quality repairs and customer service.

He added that the survey isn’t just on the top 10 national insurers; it includes smaller, regional carriers, depending on where carriers do business. Depending on where insurers do business, repairers oftentimes grade 20 or 30 carriers in their respective state.

“In past years, it’s often those smaller insurers that are among the companies receiving the highest grades from shops,” Yoswick said. “It’s a tool that shows consumers that they have more choices than they may realize and reminds them that there’s something other than just price to consider when they’re buying insurance.”
Other considerations include how insurers will handle their claim.

“That’s something shops see every day and can compare one insurer to another,” Yoswick said. “We also believe the more shops that are aware of the Insurer Report Card and that participate and use the report, the more consumers will be made aware of it. That’s our No. 1 goal — to help provide a tool for shops and consumers to use to show that there are differences among insurers.”

Around 1,100 shops typically respond to the survey each year. Yoswick said the more shops that participate, the more validity and credibility the Insurer Report Card gains. More participation also means more insurers for a consumer to learn about, he said.
Yoswick noted that insurer grades aren’t reported in the Insurer Report Card until a set minimum number of shops have graded that insurer.
“Even getting just a half dozen or 10 more shops participating in a state can add one, two, or three good insurers to the report for their particular state,” he said.
Insurers pay attention to the Insurer Report Card results and often ask for details on the “why” behind the grades they receive, Yoswick said.

“All that individual information remains strictly confidential, but when shops take the time to answer some of the follow-up questions in the survey about the insurers they graded, it helps us develop some cumulative data to show, for example, that some insurers get a low grade even from their DRP shops,” he said. “We can show that some companies get a lower grade primarily because they’re parts policies or just because their claims processes are more burdensome or just because shops see them as being less responsive than other insurers.”

He added that insurers who receive the best grades are increasingly using that in their marketing. Plus, other publications and organizations, including The Wall Street Journal, Money, and USA Today, incorporate Insurer Report Card findings into their own scoring system for auto insurers.

In addition to grading insurance companies specific to each survey respondent’s state, optional questions focus on parts policies, payment for OEM repair procedures, and delve deeper into insurer claims processes.
Yoswick says the Insurer Report Card findings are a tool for shops and trade associations to use when speaking with lawmakers or insurance regulators.

“I think a lawmaker or an insurance regulator might sometimes hear, ‘Well, all shops don’t like any insurers,’ and there’s a lot more nuance than that,” he said. “When shops are talking with regulators and lawmakers, they can use the Insurer Report Card report to show that there’s some insurers handling claims in better ways for consumers.”
He added that the Insurer Report Card includes regional data breakouts and state-specific reports when there are enough survey respondents.

According to the last Insurer Report Card, released in February, seven auto insurance companies received an A-minus or higher. Thirty-five insurers received a B or higher, earning an Honor Roll spot. Twenty-two carriers, including six of the largest U.S. auto insurers, received a C-minus or lower.
None of the top 10 largest national auto insurers received an overall grade higher than a C-plus, while more than 60 other insurers ranked higher.

Yoswick spoke about the survey at the Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ IDEAS Collide Showcase at the 2025 SEMA Show. He said thousands of consumers, insurance regulators, and insurance carriers download the report card results every year. The survey is currently in its 10th year.

Volvo and Mercedes-Benz have separately expanded their partnerships with NVIDIA to advance automated driving, according to press releases from both automakers.

The automakers will be provided with NVIDIA’s Hyperion in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture through the partnerships. They will also have access to NVIDIA’s Alpamayo Stack for full-stack driving software and AI reasoning capabilities.

Volvo says it will combine its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA’s technologies. It will enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. This will include everything from highways and busy urban streets to parking scenarios.
The automaker will also use NVIDIA’s Halo operating system.

“Volvo has been synonymous with car safety for almost 100 years,” said Håkan Samuelsson, Volvo Cars president and CEO, in the release. “By working with NVIDIA, we bring together two distinct strengths: industry-leading safety knowledge and world-class AI technology. That combination gives us a unique opportunity to create safer and more attractive cars for our customers.”
Jensen Huang, NVIDIA founder and CEO, said that accelerated computing has transformed the car into an intelligent machine.

“Volvo has spent nearly a century protecting people on the road,” Huang said. “Together, we’re combining Volvo’s extraordinary vehicle safety systems with NVIDIA Hyperion and Halos to build a new generation of cars that make driving safer and more effortless.”
The automaker plans to debut the technology in a next-generation car.
Volvo and NVIDIA have been working together since 2017.
Mercedes-Benz says its partnership with NVIDIA brings together the automaker’s engineering and safety expertise with its MB.OS operating system.

The automaker’s operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, the release states. It adds that with NVIDIA’s technologies, the system can support point-to-point urban assistance, active safety, and automated parking.

NVIDIA’s Halos builds on the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails, the release adds. Together, the technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines.

“NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving,” said Jörg Burzer, Mercedes Board of Management member and Development and Procurement chief technology officer, in the release. “Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the Western world. The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.”

Ali Kani, NVIDIA president of automotive, said, “Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.”

CCC Intelligent Solutions Inc. (CCC), has announced Calibration Guidelines, a new capability that brings recommendations from leading providers directly into existing estimating workflows.
As advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more common and complex, repairers and insurers need trusted calibration guidance at the point of decision.

“The growing complexity of today’s vehicles is raising the stakes for every participant in the repair ecosystem,” said Dan Risley, vice president, Automotive Services Group for CCC. “Supporting safe, proper and consistent repairs requires collaboration across repairers, insurers, automakers, diagnostics providers and technology partners. CCC is helping make trusted calibration guidance easier to access and apply as repair and claims decisions are being made.”

Industry stakeholders, including leading repair associations and consumer advocacy groups, have increasingly identified ADAS calibrations as one of the collision repair industry’s most pressing issues, citing the need for easier access to trusted repair guidance.

“ADAS represents one of the most significant technological changes our industry has ever faced,” said Erick Bickett, director, PACE Calibration Centers. “The pace and magnitude of this change demand collaboration across the entire industry. We appreciate CCC’s leadership in making calibration guidance more accessible at the point where critical repair decisions are made and for their work as part of CIECA’s ADAS Calibration Committee. Together, these efforts are important steps toward greater transparency and proper repairers.”

CCC’s Calibration Guidelines sources recommendations, informed by vehicle manufacturers’ repair and calibration requirements, from leading calibration and diagnostics providers. Current participants include asTech (via adasThink), Azimuth, Opus (via ADAS Map Pro), Kinetic and REVV.

“No single stakeholder can solve this challenge alone,” Risley said. “The industry’s continued focus on ADAS calibration reflects a shared commitment to consumers, safer roadways and the proper repair of increasingly sophisticated vehicles. CCC is proud to support those efforts by helping connect trusted information with the people who need it.”

Calibration Guidelines is available to all CCC ONE users at no additional cost from CCC. Customers with a contracted participating provider can access recommendations through the Diagnostics button in CCC ONE; insurers using Advanced or Intelligent Estimating in APEX can also access the capability.
Visit cccis.com/diagnostics to learn more.
